channel.title: Systemic Error
channel.description: Independent commentary by Paulo Santos on politics, power, technology, and the systems behind the headlines. This isn’t a glitch. It’s the design.

item.title: The Devil Made You Think: How Religious Clickbait Masquerades as Profound Wisdom
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: When ordinary human psychology gets repackaged as supernatural warfare, critical thinking becomes the enemy, unquestioning obedience becomes a virtue, and the Devil becomes the world's most convenient scapegoat. item.content:encoded:
When ordinary human psychology gets repackaged as supernatural warfare, critical thinking becomes the enemy, unquestioning obedience becomes a virtue, and the Devil becomes the world's most convenient scapegoat.

There is something almost impressive about the religious content industry's ability to take the most mundane observations about human existence, wrap them in biblical quotations, sprinkle a little Satan on top, and present the resulting intellectual casserole as profound spiritual revelation.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

The latest specimen comes courtesy of an MSN slideshow titled “9 Lies the Devil Wants You to Believe.”

Nine lies. Apparently, the Prince of Darkness has been reduced from the cosmic adversary of an omnipotent deity to a motivational speaker specializing in negative self-talk.

And what are these diabolical deceptions? That your past mistakes define you. That you need to handle everything yourself. That forgiveness means excusing wrongdoing. That unanswered prayers might actually be unanswered.

In other words, ordinary human insecurities, moral dilemmas, and perfectly reasonable questions.

But according to this particular brand of religious publishing, these aren't simply thoughts worth examining. They're Satanic propaganda.

And therein lies the problem.

This isn't merely harmless religious encouragement. It is an example of an extraordinarily persistent intellectual fraud: presenting theological assumptions as established facts, dressing ordinary psychological advice in supernatural authority, and treating skepticism itself as evidence of evil.

The result is an exercise in circular reasoning so thoroughly insulated from scrutiny that it could survive a direct collision with reality without developing so much as a dent.

First, Invent the Disease. Then Sell the Cure.

Consider the first supposed lie:

“Your private sin isn't affecting anybody else, so it doesn't really matter.”

The article warns that hidden moral failings gradually corrupt a person's character, diminish spiritual awareness, and eventually contaminate their relationships.

Notice what it doesn't bother establishing.

What exactly qualifies as sin? Who gets to decide? And what evidence demonstrates that every private violation of religious doctrine causes harm?

There is a fundamental distinction between immorality and disobedience to religious rules.

A person who privately exploits another human being has committed a moral wrong, regardless of whether anyone discovers it.

A person who privately entertains doubts about God has not.

Neither has someone who masturbates, engages in consensual intimacy outside marriage, or violates any number of religious prohibitions that cannot be connected to demonstrable harm.

Yet the article neatly collapses the distinction.

Once something receives the label “sin,” its moral condemnation is treated as settled. No evidence of injury is required. No injured party needs to exist. The offense is against an invisible authority whose existence and jurisdiction are themselves articles of faith.

That's not moral reasoning. That's obedience masquerading as morality.

And when the author invokes Luke 8:17 to warn that nothing hidden will remain concealed, the argument becomes even more revealing.

Apparently, the ultimate problem with private conduct isn't necessarily that it hurts someone.

It's that someone might eventually find out.

What a wonderful foundation for an ethical system.

Ordinary Psychology, Now With Added Supernatural Packaging

Several entries contain advice so unremarkable that they could have been lifted from a bargain-bin self-help book.

Your past mistakes don't have to define your future.

You don't need to be perfect before seeking compassion.

Material comfort doesn't necessarily mean you're living correctly.

Excessive independence can become exhausting.

These are not profound discoveries.

Human beings have been exploring such ideas through philosophy, literature, psychology, and ordinary conversation for centuries.

But add a biblical quotation, and suddenly they become divine revelations.

Take the claim that people shouldn't believe their past mistakes permanently limit their worth.

Excellent advice.

People can change. People can learn. People can recover from failure.

But the article doesn't simply say that.

It warns against believing that previous mistakes limit one's “usefulness to God.”

Usefulness?

What an extraordinary choice of words.

Here we have a supposedly omnipotent being who created the universe, governs reality, and requires absolutely nothing to accomplish anything.

Yet human beings are apparently expected to evaluate themselves according to their usefulness to him.

The language of human dignity has been replaced with the language of divine employment.

You aren't valuable because you're a conscious human being capable of relationships, creativity, compassion, and growth.

You're valuable because you might still be useful to the celestial management department.

How inspiring.

And the supposed solution is always the same: you need God.

Not because the author has demonstrated that the psychological benefit cannot exist without religion, but because the entire argument begins with the assumption that religion is necessary.

It's the theological equivalent of claiming that drinking water only works because an angel blesses every glass.

The water still hydrates you.

The angel is an unnecessary addition.

Forgiveness: The Perfect Tool for Protecting the Wrong People

Then comes the claim:

“If you forgive them, you are just letting them off the hook and erasing what they did.”

Here the article argues that refusing forgiveness traps people in bitterness while their offenders continue living freely.

It's a familiar religious refrain, and one that deserves substantially more scrutiny than it usually receives.

Forgiveness can be psychologically beneficial.

So can accountability.

So can distance.

So can refusing to allow a dangerous person back into your life.

What is not psychologically necessary is the belief that everyone who has harmed you deserves forgiveness.

A person can overcome anger without forgiving an abuser.

A person can build a fulfilling life without absolving someone who betrayed them.

A victim can recognize that an offender remains responsible for their actions without spending every waking moment consumed by resentment.

The article reduces these complex experiences to a convenient false choice: forgive or remain imprisoned by bitterness.

And that's where this particular religious teaching can become genuinely harmful.

In abusive families, controlling relationships, and religious institutions protecting their own reputations, the demand for forgiveness can become a weapon.

The offender asks for mercy.

The community demands reconciliation.

The victim is told that continued anger demonstrates a spiritual failing.

Suddenly, the person who suffered the injury is made responsible for restoring everyone's comfort.

Forgiveness is a personal choice, not a moral debt owed to an offender.

And no amount of scriptural quotation changes that.

When Logic Becomes the Devil's Accomplice

Of all nine entries, the seventh is perhaps the most intellectually revealing.

“You can wage war in the spiritual realm with your mind, strength and logic.”

According to the article, relying on human wisdom and psychological explanations leaves people defenseless against the spiritual forces supposedly responsible for their struggles.

Let's examine the extraordinary claim being made here.

Someone experiences anxiety.

Someone struggles with depression.

Someone has intrusive thoughts, persistent fear, or emotional exhaustion.

These experiences may have biological, psychological, environmental, or social explanations.

We can investigate them. We can test hypotheses. We can develop treatments. We can measure outcomes.

But the article introduces another explanation: invisible spiritual forces.

And how do we determine that these forces exist?

Scripture.

How do we determine scripture accurately describes reality?

Faith.

And what happens when logic leads someone to question the explanation?

Apparently, logic is the wrong weapon.

How remarkably convenient.

The moment a belief system teaches people to distrust the intellectual tools that might expose its errors, it has stopped defending truth and started defending itself.

This is not a trivial concern.

Religious faith can provide genuine psychological comfort. Many believers combine prayer with professional treatment, and the article does not explicitly tell anyone to abandon medical care.

But portraying psychological explanations as inadequate because an invisible spiritual war is supposedly taking place risks encouraging vulnerable people to misidentify the nature of their distress.

A person experiencing mental illness does not need to be told that demons might be participating.

They need compassion, competent assessment, and appropriate support.

The supernatural explanation adds fear without adding evidence.

And dismissing logic as insufficient does not transform an unsupported claim into a fact.

It merely protects that claim from examination.

The Garden of Eden: Where Asking Questions Became a Crime

Another alleged Satanic deception is that God withholds good things because he wants to restrict human happiness.

The article invokes the Garden of Eden, naturally portraying the serpent as the original manipulator who convinced humanity that divine restrictions were oppressive.

But there's an inconvenient detail in the Genesis narrative.

God forbids Adam and Eve from eating from the Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil.

The serpent tells Eve that eating the fruit will open their eyes and make them like God, knowing good and evil.

They eat.

Their eyes are opened.

And in Genesis 3:22, God declares:

“The man has now become like one of us, knowing good and evil.”

Well, that's awkward.

The serpent's prediction about acquiring knowledge is substantially confirmed within the story itself.

The narrative also involves mortality, disobedience, and consequences, so it would be simplistic to claim that everything the serpent said was true.

But the irony is difficult to ignore.

Humanity's foundational transgression, in this telling, involves acquiring knowledge that a divine authority had forbidden.

And the lesson commonly emphasized is obedience.

Don't question the rule.

Don't challenge the authority.

Don't assume restrictions might be unjustified.

Just trust the one issuing them.

That is a remarkably useful lesson for any institution that depends on unquestioning compliance.

And we should be exceptionally suspicious when religious authorities attempt to extend that principle from an ancient myth into contemporary human relationships.

A parent, employer, government, or religious leader who says, “You don't need to understand my rules; you simply need to obey them,” is not offering a compelling moral argument.

They're demanding submission.

Authority does not become legitimate merely because it claims to be benevolent.

Its decisions still require justification.

And telling people that questioning restrictions is a temptation from Satan is an excellent way to avoid providing one.

The Unanswered Prayer: A System That Cannot Lose

Finally, consider the ninth alleged lie:

“Delay means denial, so God must have forgotten about your prayers.”

According to the article, unanswered prayers don't indicate divine absence. They simply mean God's timing differs from yours.

Now consider what that interpretation accomplishes.

Someone prays for employment.

Nothing happens.

God is teaching patience.

Someone prays for recovery.

The illness progresses.

God has another plan.

Someone prays for a suffering child.

The child dies.

God works in mysterious ways.

Whatever happens, the underlying belief survives.

A favorable outcome becomes evidence of divine intervention.

An unfavorable outcome becomes evidence of divine wisdom beyond human understanding.

An absence of observable results becomes evidence that the answer hasn't arrived yet.

The proposition is structured so that no possible outcome can count against it.

And a claim that accommodates every conceivable result without distinguishing among them offers no useful predictive explanation.

This does not mean every religious person believes prayer guarantees particular results. Many sophisticated theological traditions explicitly reject that understanding.

But the article's treatment offers little more than a comforting assertion presented as an explanation.

God didn't ignore you.

God isn't late.

God has a plan.

How do we know?

Because the religion says so.

Again.

The more troubling implication is the suggestion that people who become impatient and take action may be trying to force outcomes rather than trusting divine timing.

Sometimes waiting is prudent.

Sometimes waiting is disastrous.

A person experiencing medical symptoms should seek medical attention.

Someone facing abuse should seek safety.

Someone whose livelihood is collapsing should take practical steps to protect themselves.

Prayer may offer comfort to believers, but inaction does not become wisdom merely because it has been given a religious justification.

The Devil: Christianity's Universal Technical Support Excuse

Here is the underlying brilliance of this entire rhetorical system.

Every unwanted thought can be attributed to Satan.

Every comforting thought can be attributed to God.

Every fortunate outcome can demonstrate divine favor.

Every unfortunate outcome can demonstrate divine wisdom.

Every doubt can be interpreted as spiritual attack.

And every demand for evidence can be dismissed as reliance on inadequate human understanding.

It's an intellectual machine designed to produce the same conclusion regardless of its input.

Consider the exchange:

“I don't believe Satan exists.”

That's exactly what Satan wants you to believe.

“I don't believe the Bible is divinely inspired.”

Satan is deceiving you.

“I've examined the evidence and found the claims unconvincing.”

You're relying too much on human logic.

“What evidence would demonstrate that your explanation is wrong?”

You need faith.

The argument isn't merely circular.

It's self-sealing.

It converts every objection into additional confirmation.

And that's precisely what distinguishes an honest investigation from an ideological system designed to protect itself.

An honest investigation permits the possibility that its initial assumptions are mistaken.

This kind of religious argument makes that possibility practically unavailable.

The Real Problem Isn't Faith. It's Intellectual Dishonesty.

People are entitled to religious beliefs.

They're entitled to find meaning in scripture, comfort in prayer, and guidance in spiritual traditions.

They're even entitled to believe that Satan personally spends his afternoons planting insecurities in the human mind.

But belief is not evidence.

And faith-based interpretations should not be presented to a general audience as though they were established descriptions of reality.

There is an enormous difference between saying:

“My religious tradition teaches that these thoughts may represent spiritual temptation.”

And declaring:

“These are nine lies the Devil wants you to believe.”

The first is an honest statement about religious belief.

The second presents a supernatural claim as fact without demonstrating that it is true.

That distinction is not pedantic.

It's the difference between explaining a worldview and attempting to impose its assumptions on reality.

What makes this particular genre so irritating is how often it borrows credibility from genuine psychological insights.

Yes, excessive self-criticism can be destructive.

Yes, isolation can worsen anxiety.

Yes, forgiveness can sometimes contribute to healing.

Yes, past mistakes need not determine a person's future.

But none of those observations establishes that Satan exists.

None demonstrates that a supernatural intelligence implants thoughts.

And none proves that the Bible is an authoritative account of human psychology.

A correct observation does not validate every explanation attached to it.

If someone tells you that exercise improves health because invisible angels massage your cardiovascular system, the demonstrated benefits of exercise do not establish the existence of the angels.

Yet religious clickbait routinely performs exactly that maneuver.

Take a genuine human experience.

Attach an unverifiable supernatural explanation.

Quote scripture.

Declare victory.

Publish.

Repeat.

The Business of Manufacturing Profundity

There is also something particularly cynical about the presentation.

Nine lies.

Nine things Satan wants you to believe.

Nine hidden spiritual dangers threatening your happiness, relationships, and salvation.

The format is practically indistinguishable from the endless internet slideshows promising “Ten Secrets Doctors Don't Want You to Know” or “Seven Habits That Are Secretly Destroying Your Brain.”

Only here, instead of medical professionals supposedly concealing information, we have the Devil.

And instead of offering evidence, the article offers Bible verses.

It's religious engagement bait: familiar anxieties packaged as supernatural revelations, designed to sound urgent and profound.

The reader arrives with ordinary human uncertainties and leaves with a new interpretive framework in which those uncertainties may be evidence of cosmic malevolence.

What an extraordinary service.

Take someone's existing insecurity.

Tell them an invisible enemy is exploiting it.

Then direct them toward the belief system that claims exclusive knowledge of the enemy and the means to resist him.

This doesn't mean every author producing devotional content is consciously manipulating readers. Many undoubtedly believe what they're writing.

Sincerity, however, does not rescue an argument from intellectual bankruptcy.

And the fact that such content appears on mainstream news aggregators only adds another layer of absurdity.

Religious devotional writing is being distributed alongside news and general-interest articles, potentially reaching readers without much indication that its foundational claims are matters of faith rather than independently established facts.

The medium lends the material an appearance of informational legitimacy that the argument itself has not earned.

Stop Calling Unsupported Assertions “Deep Truths”

The most exhausting feature of this genre is its insistence on presenting ancient theological assumptions as if they were astonishing insights into human nature.

You're insecure?

Satan.

You're angry?

Satan.

You're questioning authority?

Satan.

You're trying to solve problems through reason?

Believe it or not, Satan.

Meanwhile, God is credited with comfort, forgiveness, patience, and every positive personal transformation the author can identify.

It's a cosmic accounting system where the books are guaranteed to balance because the rules determine the outcome in advance.

And beneath the theological decoration lies a deeply consequential message:

Your thoughts are not always trustworthy.

Your judgment may be compromised by invisible enemies.

Your understanding is inadequate.

Your doubts are suspicious.

Your safest option is to trust the religious framework explaining all of this.

That is not necessarily how every reader will interpret the article. But it is a disturbing pattern embedded in its reasoning.

Healthy skepticism doesn't require rejecting every piece of advice contained in religious literature.

It requires distinguishing the advice from the unsupported supernatural claims used to justify it.

You can recognize the value of forgiveness without believing in demons.

You can acknowledge that excessive independence causes stress without surrendering your autonomy to a deity.

You can learn from mistakes without considering yourself a sinner in need of supernatural redemption.

You can accept uncertainty without inventing a cosmic plan.

And you can confront emotional distress without imagining an invisible war being fought inside your skull.

Human beings are complicated.

We experience fear, guilt, hope, love, anger, doubt, and uncertainty because we are human.

We don't need to outsource the explanation of those experiences to competing supernatural entities.

Sometimes a troubling thought is simply a troubling thought.

Sometimes an unanswered prayer is simply an unanswered prayer.

Sometimes a restriction is genuinely unjustified.

And sometimes the person telling you not to trust your own reasoning is the person whose claims deserve the most scrutiny.

The Devil doesn't need to be deceiving you for religious propaganda to be misleading.

Human beings are perfectly capable of doing that all by themselves.

And unlike Satan, we can actually hold them accountable.

It’s the design.

item.title: Top historian: Trump conceded on Election Night —but the danger isn’t over
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: AlterNet reports that Donald Trump conceded after Democrats won commanding majorities in both chambers of Congress in the 2026 midterms, despite later posting that the elections were rigged. item.content:encoded:
AlterNet reports that Donald Trump conceded after Democrats won commanding majorities in both chambers of Congress in the 2026 midterms, despite later posting that the elections were rigged. The immediate result is clear: Democrats are set to take control of the House and Senate. The political meaning is less comforting. Trump’s relatively restrained Election Night response did not erase his record of trying to overturn the 2020 presidential election, and his selection of Stephen Miller as chief of staff points toward confrontation, not accommodation, during his remaining two years in office.

Historian Federico Finchelstein’s warning is straightforward: accepting a defeat that cannot plausibly be reversed is not the same as accepting democratic limits. Trump may have yielded to the scale of the result while retaining the authoritarian politics that made another attempted power grab a reasonable concern in the first place.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

A concession imposed by arithmetic

The precise character of Trump’s reported concession is not described in the supplied account. AlterNet says he conceded, while also noting that he subsequently alleged the midterms were rigged. That is materially different from a democratic leader acknowledging the legitimacy of an election and the authority voters transferred to the opposition.

Finchelstein, an historian of fascism and author of A Brief History of Fascist Lies and The Wannabe Fascists, told AlterNet that Trump appeared surprised by the result. He cited an unnamed person close to Trump who reportedly described the Democratic victory as “too big to rig.” Finchelstein presented that as a possible explanation for Trump’s delayed and initially less hostile response.

The phrase captures the limit Trump encountered: not principle, but scale. On Finchelstein’s reading, the vote produced a reality too overwhelming for Trump’s usual machinery of denial to contest effectively. That interpretation remains an interpretation, not a demonstrated account of Trump’s private reasoning. But it fits the public contradiction AlterNet describes—a reported concession followed by another unsupported claim that an election he lost was rigged.

Trump’s conduct after the 2020 election supplies the relevant context. He attempted to remain in power after losing, culminating in the effort to overturn the result associated with January 6. Against that record, a quieter response in 2026 cannot reasonably be treated as evidence that he has become committed to democratic succession.

Miller’s promotion answers the reconciliation question

The clearest reported indication of Trump’s intended course is personnel. After voters rejected his governing coalition and handed Congress to Democrats, Trump chose Stephen Miller as his chief of staff. Finchelstein characterized Miller as perhaps one of the most fascistic figures in the administration and described the appointment as an almost immediate turn toward radicalization.

That decision matters more than the fleeting presidential tone celebrated by pundits. A chief of staff controls access, coordinates policy and helps determine which impulses become government action. By elevating Miller, Trump did not signal that he intended to bargain with the incoming congressional majorities. He placed a central architect of his hard-line politics near the core of executive power.

Finchelstein expects the conflict to intensify as Trump confronts the gap between his self-image and his diminished position. Trump urged voters to treat the midterms as a referendum on him; they returned Democratic majorities in both houses. He is now a lame-duck president who built his politics around personal dominance and the leader cult Finchelstein identifies as central to Trumpism.

“The less power he has,” Finchelstein told AlterNet, “the more potential for violence, erratic behavior and illegality we might have.” That is a forecast, not a report of acts that have already occurred. But Congress changing hands does not itself remove the executive authority Trump retains until his term ends. It changes the institutional balance and creates stronger legislative opposition; it does not make presidential power disappear.

The myth behind the program

Finchelstein describes Trumpism as “wannabe fascism”: an aspiration marked by fascist tendencies that remains incomplete, erratic and perhaps incapable of full realization. The distinction is useful because it avoids treating fascism as a costume that either fits perfectly or not at all. The relevant question is what Trump’s movement attempts to do with the power it possesses.

One element is a politics of national rebirth built around a fabricated past. Trump presents himself as the agent who can restore an earlier American greatness while remaking the country through architectural projects and the removal of so-called DEI material from public monuments. Finchelstein argues that the glorious past invoked by this project never existed as advertised. Whatever prosperity or status it offered some Americans came with exclusion and suffering for others.

That mythology has an immediate political function. It defines the nation narrowly, casts selected groups as intruders or contaminants, and gives the leader permission to “restore” a social order that exists mainly as propaganda. Finchelstein calls Trump’s conception of the nation extremely chauvinistic and exclusionary. The invented history is not decorative rhetoric around the governing program; it supplies the program’s justification.

Congress won power, not automatic compliance

AlterNet asked whether Democratic control of Congress had permanently prevented Trump from attacking democratic institutions, including through emergency powers, martial law or an attempt to entrench one-party rule. Finchelstein did not claim those outcomes were imminent. He said they could not be ruled out, given Trump’s prior conduct and the history of authoritarian movements.

That is the properly bounded warning. The election created a substantial institutional obstacle to Trump, and voters denied him the mandate he sought. It did not retroactively change his behavior after the 2020 election, convert him into a conventional lame duck or guarantee that every part of the state apparatus will resist an unlawful demand.

The most revealing misdirection came in the first hours after the defeat, when, according to Finchelstein, media figures and pundits began imagining that Trump’s initial response marked his transformation into a responsible presidential leader. That familiar ritual grants the powerful rehabilitation for briefly refraining from their worst expected conduct. It treats compliance with an election result as statesmanship rather than the minimum obligation of anyone entrusted with public office.

Finchelstein argues that resistance now depends not only on voters reiterating what they already decided, but on Congress and other state officials enforcing that decision. Voters transferred legislative power. Whether that verdict constrains Trump will also depend on officials with actual institutional authority refusing to assist any renewed attempt to evade it.

The Democratic victory therefore settled who will control Congress. It did not settle how a president who still calls elections rigged, previously tried to overturn a defeat and has now elevated Stephen Miller will use the power he retains. Trump’s reported concession closed the count. It did not close the danger.

It’s the design.

item.title: NYT columnist reveals key to halting Trump’s 'real and serious' 2028 plot
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: The most important obstacle to any attempt by President Donald Trump to subvert the 2028 election may now sit outside Washington: Democratic control of state governments in swing states and in Maryland and Virginia, the states bordering the capital. item.content:encoded:
The most important obstacle to any attempt by President Donald Trump to subvert the 2028 election may now sit outside Washington: Democratic control of state governments in swing states and in Maryland and Virginia, the states bordering the capital. New York Times columnist Jamelle Bouie argues that recent midterm victories gave Democrats both the authority to administer crucial elections and a defensive perimeter against federal interference. That is the “key” promised by the headline—not a procedural trick, but control of institutions capable of refusing an unlawful power grab.

State victories became election infrastructure

In a YouTube installment of his “Takes” series, Bouie emphasized that Democratic gains at the state level included governing trifectas, giving the party control of both legislative chambers and the governorship in several states. Those governments can enact policies that Trump could obstruct at the federal level. More urgently, they will oversee parts of the electoral machinery on which the 2028 presidential contest depends.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

“It really matters who holds these seats,” Bouie said. “It also matters a great deal for the 2028 election.”

That point cuts through a persistent weakness in national political coverage: its fixation on the White House and Congress as though state officials were spectators. Presidential elections are administered through state institutions. The people controlling those institutions can defend lawful results—or become pressure points for a president seeking to overturn them.

According to Bouie, Democrats now lead all the major swing states, as well as Maryland and Virginia on Washington’s borders. He described that alignment as important to “maintaining the integrity of elections” and ensuring that they remain free and fair.

These victories do not make election subversion impossible. They do, however, deny Trump an easier path through compliant state governments. Political control is not merely symbolic when officials may be asked to resist intimidation, reject manufactured disputes or defend certified outcomes.

Bouie expects the danger to peak in 2028

Bouie distinguished the midterms from the next presidential transition. He said he was “very confident that Trump will attempt real and serious shenanigans for 2028 in a way that they didn’t quite do for 2026.”

That is a prediction, not a report of an established plan. AlterNet’s headline inflates it into Trump’s “2028 plot,” although the supplied reporting identifies no specific operation. What Bouie describes is a foreseeable danger rooted in Trump’s past conduct and the stakes of surrendering the presidency—not a disclosed blueprint.

“The prospect of him leaving, of him sacrificing power, of him giving it up, I think puts us all into a danger zone,” Bouie said.

His warning draws its force from January 6, when Trump’s refusal to accept his 2020 defeat culminated in the attack on the Capitol. Trump later returned to the White House and repeatedly entertained talk of a third term, despite the Constitution’s two-term limit. Some Republicans indulged that rhetoric before Trump backed away from it.

The retreat does not erase the institutional question. Term limits answer whether Trump may lawfully win another presidential term; they do not guarantee that he would cooperate with a transfer of power after the 2028 election. Bouie’s concern is therefore less about campaign speculation than about what an incumbent president might do when the legal end of his tenure becomes unavoidable.

A safeguard is not a guarantee

The political significance of the Democratic state victories lies in who can say no. Governors, legislators and election officials possess powers that cannot simply be replaced by television commentary, congressional outrage or confidence that norms will enforce themselves.

But treating Democratic control as the solution would repeat another familiar error: confusing possession of authority with willingness to use it. State governments can strengthen election administration, prepare for litigation and resist federal pressure. They cannot, by themselves, neutralize every lever available to an incumbent president or ensure that national institutions will hold.

The clearer lesson is that election protection depends on power being held by officials prepared to defend the result. Bouie’s case is strongest there. The midterms did not expose a specific Trump plot, much less halt one in advance. They changed the institutional terrain on which any attempt to retain power would have to operate—and placed more of that terrain beyond Trump’s direct control.

item.title: US soldier handed over to Americans over Russia spying
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: A U.S. Army lieutenant colonel assigned to a NATO headquarters in Britain has been transferred from British counterterrorism custody to the U.S. military amid allegations that he assisted Russian intelligence. item.content:encoded:
A U.S. Army lieutenant colonel assigned to a NATO headquarters in Britain has been transferred from British counterterrorism custody to the U.S. military amid allegations that he assisted Russian intelligence. The handover does not resolve the case against Lt. Col. Brandon Carroll Tyner. It shifts the investigation to the institution that entrusted him with access to sensitive military information—and whose security procedures are now under scrutiny alongside his alleged conduct.

Tyner, 41, was arrested near Gloucester by British counterterrorism police. According to the BBC, he had been based at Imjin Barracks in Innsworth, Gloucestershire, headquarters of NATO’s Allied Rapid Reaction Corps, a unit positioned close to the alliance’s military planning and operational coordination.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

He remains accused, not convicted. Authorities have not publicly specified what information he allegedly obtained or disclosed.

Britain hands the investigation to the U.S. military

British police initially arrested Tyner under two provisions of the National Security Act 2023: one concerning the obtaining or disclosure of protected information, and another covering assistance to a foreign intelligence service. Officers also searched two locations in Gloucestershire as part of the investigation.

Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, who leads Britain’s Counter Terrorism Policing, said officials subsequently decided to let their American counterparts advance the case. The Metropolitan Police described the transfer as consistent with international protocols.

“These are extremely serious allegations,” Taylor said, adding that the joint response was intended to demonstrate that suspected espionage would be met “swiftly and robustly.”

That institutional language is emphatic but limited. A transfer of custody is not a finding of guilt, and a display of allied coordination cannot answer the central security question: whether a senior officer inside a strategically important NATO command provided Russia with protected information—and, if so, how he evaded the safeguards designed to prevent precisely that outcome.

The alleged breach came from inside NATO’s perimeter

The political significance of the case lies in Tyner’s position. He was not an outsider accused of trying to penetrate a military installation. He was a senior serviceman placed inside one, reportedly trusted with sensitive material at a headquarters serving NATO’s Allied Rapid Reaction Corps.

“The alleged conduct of a senior soldier, entrusted with sensitive information, is a sobering reminder that insider threats are real and persistent,” said Brig. Gen. Sean Stinchon, commander of U.S. Army Counterintelligence Command.

That is an accurate description of the danger, but it also points back at the military’s own responsibilities. Stinchon urged personnel to report suspicious activity to counterintelligence offices. Reporting matters, yet the military cannot reduce an alleged failure involving a lieutenant colonel to whether individual witnesses spoke up. Senior officers receive access because institutions vet, monitor and continually assess them. When that trust is allegedly abused, the scrutiny belongs not only on the accused but also on the system that granted and maintained his access.

National security analyst Mick Mulroy told ABC News that Tyner would have received continuing counterintelligence briefings because Russian efforts to penetrate the unit were foreseeable. If the allegations are substantiated, the case would therefore involve no novel or hidden danger. It would represent a possible breach by the very adversary that officials had already identified and warned personnel about.

Two governments retain an interest in the case

A person with direct knowledge of the matter told ABC News that Tyner faces action from both British authorities and the U.S. Army because the suspected disclosures concerned American and British military activity. The specific charges he could ultimately face were unclear at the time of his arrest. Under the American military justice system, an espionage conviction can carry a sentence of up to life imprisonment.

Those distinctions matter. Tyner’s arrest under British national-security law establishes the basis on which police detained him, not that the allegations have been proved. His transfer places him in U.S. military custody, but it does not erase Britain’s stated interest or predetermine what either government will charge.

The suspected target gives the case consequences beyond an ordinary personnel scandal. Russia is waging war against Ukraine, which the United States and Britain support. Information about allied military planning could aid Moscow and obstruct that support, depending on what was allegedly shared. The reporting does not establish that any particular operation was compromised.

For now, the governments involved have demonstrated that they can coordinate a handover. The harder test is whether they can establish what happened, account for any institutional failure that enabled it, and prosecute the case without substituting declarations of vigilance for evidence.

item.title: Josh Hawley doesn't seem to believe Trump's tech outage explanation
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Josh Hawley did not accept the administration’s account of a series of Federal Aviation Administration outages. At a Tuesday press briefing, the Republican senator from Missouri called the proposed technical explanation — involving a router at an Arkansas radio facility and a radar site in Amarillo, Texas — “a little hard to believe” and demanded a briefing for the full Senate. That is a challenge to the administration’s transparency, but it is not, by itself, evidence that President Donald Trum
item.content:encoded:
Josh Hawley did not accept the administration’s account of a series of Federal Aviation Administration outages. At a Tuesday press briefing, the Republican senator from Missouri called the proposed technical explanation — involving a router at an Arkansas radio facility and a radar site in Amarillo, Texas — “a little hard to believe” and demanded a briefing for the full Senate.

That is a challenge to the administration’s transparency, but it is not, by itself, evidence that President Donald Trump has lost his hold on the Republican Party. AlterNet frames Hawley’s remarks that way. The reported facts establish something narrower: one of Trump’s most reliable Senate allies publicly rejected official reassurance and said Congress and the public were being kept in the dark.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Hawley rejects coincidence as an answer

According to The Hill’s Mira Bhakta, FAA officials had identified the Arkansas router and the Amarillo radar site as likely causes of an excessive flood of data that led the agency to shut down its systems. Hawley questioned whether that account could explain the broader pattern of outages.

“Maybe it’s because you know somebody unplugged a router in Arkansas or whatever,” he said. “I don’t know. I find that, frankly, a little hard to believe.”

Hawley did not offer evidence of an alternative cause. He did, however, identify the institutional failure that officials still control: senators have not received an explanation he considers adequate. “The full Senate ought to be briefed on what exactly is going on,” he said.

He later described coincidence as implausible, arguing that “all of this” could not simply be happenstance. That rhetoric goes further than the information presented in the report. Suspicion is not a technical finding, and Hawley’s disbelief does not disprove the FAA’s assessment. But the burden of explaining outages in critical aviation infrastructure belongs to the administration and the agency operating it, not to travelers asked to trust an unexplained chain of failures.

A loyalist’s dissent has limits

Hawley’s criticism carries political weight because he has repeatedly helped sustain Trump’s power. He backed Trump’s false claim that the 2020 election was stolen and, after Republican losses in the 2026 midterm elections, announced a brief fast in response to what he called a “shocking and historic” result.

His record also includes conduct with consequences beyond partisan theater. In July, former Justice Department lawyer Elizabeth Oyer accused Hawley and fellow Missouri Republican Sen. Eric Schmitt of inciting violence against her during a hearing. Oyer said in a YouTube video that she began receiving death threats after testifying against Todd Blanche. That remains her allegation; the supplied reporting does not establish that either senator directed or intended the threats.

Hawley has broken with Trump before. He joined Democrats in condemning the president’s reported unauthorized invasion of Venezuela. He has also criticized other Trump-aligned Republicans for failing to impose further restrictions on access to reproductive technology after the overturning of Roe v. Wade, telling Axios in December that conservatives needed a stronger cultural voice “advocating for life.”

Those departures show that Hawley is capable of dissent when it serves his own political agenda. They do not establish a general rupture with Trump. Republican power is not measured by whether every senator accepts every administration explanation; it is measured by what lawmakers are willing to investigate, obstruct, expose, or ultimately permit.

The unanswered question is institutional

The most consequential part of Hawley’s statement is not his speculation about coincidence. It is his assertion that elected lawmakers and the public lack a sufficient account of failures affecting federal aviation systems.

If the FAA’s technical explanation is correct, the administration should be able to brief Congress on how the failures occurred, why they produced such serious disruption, and what safeguards are being imposed. If the explanation is incomplete, congressional scrutiny should establish what officials omitted and why.

For now, the report documents a demand for answers, not the answers themselves — and certainly not a demonstrated collapse of Trump’s Republican support. Hawley has voiced doubt. Whether that doubt matters will depend on whether the Senate forces disclosure or allows one skeptical press-briefing performance to substitute for oversight.

item.title: Trump victim of ‘most stunning geopolitical coup’ ever: analysis
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: AlterNet’s headline casts Donald Trump as the victim of a geopolitical coup. The analysis it describes says almost the opposite: Jonathan V. Last, writing in The Bulwark , argues that Trump has made the United States a willing partner of authoritarian powers, allowing Vladimir Putin’s Russia and Xi Jinping’s China to gain American alignment without surrendering their relationship with Iran. That is not a story about something done to Trump. It is an accusation about what Trump, as president, is
item.content:encoded:
AlterNet’s headline casts Donald Trump as the victim of a geopolitical coup. The analysis it describes says almost the opposite: Jonathan V. Last, writing in The Bulwark, argues that Trump has made the United States a willing partner of authoritarian powers, allowing Vladimir Putin’s Russia and Xi Jinping’s China to gain American alignment without surrendering their relationship with Iran.

That is not a story about something done to Trump. It is an accusation about what Trump, as president, is doing with American power.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

From a loose slogan to an authoritarian partnership

Last begins with George W. Bush’s “Axis of Evil,” the label his administration applied in 2002 to Iraq, Iran and North Korea. Even on its own terms, Last writes, that grouping was incoherent. Iran and Iraq were enemies, while North Korea sold assistance to governments willing to pay. They were repressive states, but not a functioning alliance.

The more consequential alignment, in Last’s account, emerged later among Russia, China and Iran. By 2012, he argues, the three governments had spent years developing relationships intended to constrain liberal powers.

That distinction matters. Bush’s phrase bundled adversaries together for the political purposes of the War on Terror. Last is describing something more concrete: governments coordinating where their interests overlap, despite differences among them.

But he also revives Bush’s morally loaded terminology, which risks flattening distinct relationships into another sweeping civilizational camp. The useful question is not whether every government fits neatly inside an “evil” axis. It is how state power is being exercised, which partnerships it strengthens and whose interests those choices serve.

The charge against Trump

Last’s central claim is that Russia did not need to defeat the United States because it managed to “flip it.” He characterizes the Trump administration as a Putin-controlled regime and presents Trump’s reported meeting with Xi in Shenzhen that Thursday as the moment the new alignment would become visible.

“Putin and Xi” had effectively exchanged Iran for “Donald Trump’s America,” Last writes, calling the development “the most stunning geopolitical coup” ever. He further argues that Russia and China achieved this without abandoning Iran, even as, in his description, America was at war with it.

The supplied reporting does not detail the policies, agreements or concessions underlying that assessment. It does establish that Last’s argument concerns Trump’s use of the presidency, not Trump being personally duped or overpowered. His language is polemical, but the institutional structure is plain: the president controls the foreign-policy machinery of the United States. Putin and Xi may benefit from Trump’s decisions; they do not issue those decisions from the Oval Office.

Calling Trump the “victim” therefore redirects attention from the officeholder exercising American power to the foreign leaders allegedly profiting from it. That framing grants Trump passivity precisely where Last assigns him agency.

A headline that reverses the allegation

There is a legitimate argument to examine in Last’s commentary: whether Trump’s foreign policy weakens traditional liberal alliances while improving the strategic position of authoritarian governments. AlterNet’s account, however, supplies more invective than policy evidence. “Puppet regime” and “idiot president” communicate Last’s judgment; they do not, by themselves, demonstrate the mechanism of the alleged geopolitical realignment.

The headline makes the distortion worse. A president who chooses accommodation, alignment or deference is not necessarily the casualty of those choices. The country whose power he directs may bear the consequences. Allies may face them. People subjected to the strengthened reach of repressive governments may face them. But the reporting presented here does not establish Trump as the coup’s victim.

Last’s actual accusation is harsher: Trump is the means by which the supposed coup succeeds. If that accusation is to carry more than rhetorical force, it must rest on the president’s concrete decisions and their beneficiaries. The “victim” framing obscures exactly that chain of responsibility.

item.title: Senator rages at Trump nominee at live hearing: 'It’s absurd!'
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand’s objection to Hung Cao, President Donald Trump’s nominee for Navy secretary, was not about decorum. It was about Cao’s attempt to recast eight suicide attempts aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln as evidence that the Navy’s support system worked. For an administration already accused of dismissing the sailors’ suffering and restricting congressional scrutiny, the language was more than callous: it converted institutional failure into a management success. The sailors endured
item.content:encoded:
Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand’s objection to Hung Cao, President Donald Trump’s nominee for Navy secretary, was not about decorum. It was about Cao’s attempt to recast eight suicide attempts aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln as evidence that the Navy’s support system worked. For an administration already accused of dismissing the sailors’ suffering and restricting congressional scrutiny, the language was more than callous: it converted institutional failure into a management success.

The sailors endured a 321-day deployment that was extended twice, according to AlterNet. Food ran low. One service member lost 45 pounds, Gillibrand said, while families sent care packages to keep those aboard fed, functioning and physically capable of doing their jobs. Against that record, Cao offered an extraordinary accounting.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

“You see, as eight suicide attempts, I see as eight suicide mitigations because of the chaplains we have on board, the deployment resiliency counselors, as well as mental health specialists,” he said. Cao added that carrier strike groups on deployment normally experience “about one or two suicides.”

That comparison does not lessen the severity of eight attempts. It reveals the standard Cao chose: not whether commanders subjected sailors to intolerable conditions, but whether those conditions produced fewer deaths than he implied might otherwise be expected.

Turning breakdown into a performance metric

Gillibrand, a New York Democrat, said Cao was “absolutely not” suited to lead the Navy. She accused him of displaying callousness and failing to understand the needs of deployed personnel.

“Literally calling suicide attempts mitigation. It’s absurd,” she said.

The absurdity lies in the institutional sleight of hand. Chaplains, counselors and mental-health specialists may have helped prevent deaths; Cao’s statement credits their intervention. But successful emergency intervention does not vindicate the conditions that created the emergency. Calling the attempts “mitigations” shifts attention from sailors driven to crisis toward an organization congratulating itself for catching some of them before they died.

It also reduces human suffering to an outcome on an administrative ledger. Under that logic, a sailor’s suicide attempt can become evidence of resilience programming rather than a warning about command decisions, deployment extensions, shortages and the cumulative strain imposed on the crew.

Gillibrand made the material conditions central to her criticism. Families were not merely offering comforts from home, by her account. They were sending supplies needed to keep service members alive and able to work. Cao’s framing asks those sailors and families to view the absence of completed suicides not as the narrow avoidance of catastrophe, but as proof that the institution performed well.

Denial above, exclusion around it

Gillibrand said she also intended to press Cao about Trump calling reports that service members were committing suicide “fake news” and about Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s reported claim that the story was made up.

“How can he stand by Secretary Pete Hegseth, who said this was all made up?” she asked. “These are leaders who are not taking the sacrifice of our service members seriously, and that’s unacceptable.”

The administration’s posture, as described in the report, follows a recognizable progression: deny the damaging account, redefine the evidence that cannot be ignored, and restrict the opposition’s access to information needed for oversight. Host Peter Alexander noted that the administration and Defense Department had refused for months to brief Democrats about events. Republican Sen. Mike Rounds of South Dakota reportedly acknowledged that Democrats had been excluded from classified discussions.

Gillibrand said she raised the matter directly with Rounds and called the exclusion “disgraceful.” Her question was properly aimed at the official controlling access: why was the Trump administration withholding a classified briefing from Democratic senators?

Classified information is not the personal property of a president, defense secretary or congressional majority. Cutting opposition lawmakers out of briefings weakens Congress’s ability to test official claims precisely when senior officials are disputing accounts of severe harm to service members. The exclusion does not establish what happened aboard the Abraham Lincoln, but it concentrates control over the story in the same executive branch whose conduct is under scrutiny.

Accountability deferred

Gillibrand called for Hegseth to face accountability for what she described as his inability to lead troops and establish policy supporting service members. She said she believed a new Congress would investigate his leadership and the treatment of personnel deployed around the world.

That leaves the immediate power imbalance intact. Sailors bore the prolonged deployment, food shortages and mental-health crisis. Their families supplied what they could from outside. Administration officials retained control over the Pentagon, its explanations and access to classified information. Cao, seeking authority over the Navy, responded to eight suicide attempts by renaming them.

Whether the interventions aboard the carrier prevented deaths is one question. Whether the people who imposed and managed those conditions should be allowed to count the resulting crises as institutional successes is another. Cao’s answer supplied Gillibrand’s objection for her: a nominee prepared to treat attempted suicides as favorable statistics is already speaking in the language institutions use to escape responsibility.

item.title: DOJ humiliated as judge jokes about Trump’s blabbing in revenge probe
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Chief Judge James Boasberg did not expose a Justice Department humiliation so much as a breakdown in the department’s excuse: the government wants secrecy for an investigation that President Donald Trump and senior administration officials have already discussed in public. At a Tuesday hearing, Boasberg considered whether to unseal records supporting the Oct. 12 search of Rep. Ilhan Omar’s Washington home. He has not yet ordered the full warrant file released and indicated that substantial porti
item.content:encoded:
Chief Judge James Boasberg did not expose a Justice Department humiliation so much as a breakdown in the department’s excuse: the government wants secrecy for an investigation that President Donald Trump and senior administration officials have already discussed in public. At a Tuesday hearing, Boasberg considered whether to unseal records supporting the Oct. 12 search of Rep. Ilhan Omar’s Washington home. He has not yet ordered the full warrant file released and indicated that substantial portions may remain sealed.

The revealing exchange came when a Justice Department lawyer said she could not control public remarks by Trump, Vice President JD Vance and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin about the investigation’s focus. “Seems to be a common refrain,” Boasberg replied, according to Politico reporter Kyle Cheney.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

That was a joke, but the institutional problem was not funny. The administration’s most powerful officials can publicize allegations against a political adversary while the department conducting the investigation asks a court to preserve secrecy around the evidence, witnesses and legal basis for its actions.

Public accusation, private justification

The New York Times, Judicial Watch and 14 press organizations have asked Boasberg to unseal the warrant used to search Omar’s home. The Justice Department argues that the warrant has not been fully executed. Boasberg questioned that characterization, distinguishing the October search from the government’s continuing review of the seized material.

That review involves the Constitution’s Speech or Debate Clause, which protects legislative work from executive intrusion. According to Boasberg, most of the briefing and prior orders address that protection. He described the remaining dispute as a set of “purely legal questions” concerning the privilege’s reach, its application in this case and the procedures the government must follow.

This distinction matters. Calling the warrant unexecuted allows the department to describe an already completed search as unfinished, potentially strengthening its argument for continued secrecy. Boasberg’s questioning stripped away that convenient blur: agents executed the search in October; the government is now sorting through what it took and confronting constitutional limits on its access.

The judge nevertheless identified legitimate interests in withholding some material. He said the 67-page application contains significant information about the investigation’s scope, along with witnesses whose identities and roles should not yet be revealed. He is considering a partial release, not indiscriminate disclosure.

That is a more consequential story than the headline’s spectacle of bureaucratic embarrassment. A judge is weighing public access against an active investigation and witness protection while policing the executive branch’s treatment of constitutionally protected legislative material.

A prosecution apparatus with political sponsorship

Federal investigators are examining alleged discrepancies in Omar’s financial disclosures and whether her father misstated her age in citizenship documents, AlterNet reported. The Justice Department has told the court that the investigation reaches “other individuals,” and a court filing said Attorney General Todd Blanche approved the warrant.

Omar denies wrongdoing and says the Trump administration is targeting her politically. No finding reported in the source establishes that she committed either financial or immigration fraud.

The administration has nonetheless supplied the investigation with an extraordinary punitive frame. Border czar Tom Homan has said Omar could face denaturalization and deportation if investigators uncover evidence of immigration fraud. The conditional language is important: Homan described what could follow a finding, not a result investigators have already reached. But the intervention still places the machinery of citizenship revocation and expulsion into public discussion before the reported allegations have been proved.

That is where power lies in this case. Omar can deny the claims and contest the search. The administration controls the Justice Department, federal investigators and immigration enforcement, while its leading officials possess an unmatched platform for broadcasting suspicion. When those officials speak, they do not act as detached commentators on a process beyond their reach. They lead the government operating that process.

The department lawyer may genuinely lack authority to silence the president or his senior officials. Her lack of control, however, is not the same thing as the administration lacking agency. It means the official defending secrecy in court is institutionally subordinate to people who can discuss the investigation publicly without bearing the immediate burden of reconciling those remarks with the government’s legal position.

Boasberg returns to the target list

The hearing also unfolded against the administration’s prior campaign against Boasberg. In March 2025, he temporarily blocked deportation flights carrying people the government alleged were Venezuelan gang members. Trump responded by calling him a “Radical Left Lunatic” and demanding his removal from the bench.

Sen. Eric Schmitt later proposed legislation branded the “Boasberg Act,” which would require random assignment of federal district court cases. Whatever policy argument its sponsors may make for random assignment, naming the proposal after a judge attacked by the president turns court administration into personalized political punishment.

Now Boasberg is reviewing a search approved at the highest level of the Justice Department and directed at one of Trump’s prominent political antagonists. His task is narrower than the surrounding political conflict: determine which records may be released, protect witnesses where warranted and resolve the Speech or Debate Clause questions raised by the government’s review.

The court has not decided the underlying allegations against Omar, and Boasberg’s quip did not do so either. What it exposed was the administration’s asymmetrical arrangement: senior officials can amplify an investigation’s accusations, threaten its most severe possible consequences and attack the judge supervising it, while the Justice Department arrives in court insisting that the supporting record must largely remain beyond public view.

item.title: Trump shifts legal strategy in golf course fight
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: The Justice Department is no longer concentrating on persuading Judge Ana Reyes to bless the Trump administration’s stated rationale for closing the East Potomac Park golf course. According to a joint status report filed Tuesday and described by Politico’s Josh Gerstein, government lawyers instead want to waive a preliminary-injunction hearing, finish briefing by Nov. 25 and obtain a ruling before a temporary restraining order expires Nov. 28. The shift would limit the time available to examine
item.content:encoded:
The Justice Department is no longer concentrating on persuading Judge Ana Reyes to bless the Trump administration’s stated rationale for closing the East Potomac Park golf course. According to a joint status report filed Tuesday and described by Politico’s Josh Gerstein, government lawyers instead want to waive a preliminary-injunction hearing, finish briefing by Nov. 25 and obtain a ruling before a temporary restraining order expires Nov. 28. The shift would limit the time available to examine whether federal officials manufactured a safety justification after President Donald Trump had already ordered the course redeveloped.

The course closed Nov. 15. Trump’s plan would replace the inexpensive, heavily used public facility with a championship-level, PGA-style course occupying the island and capable of hosting official tournaments. That is not merely a redesign. It is a transfer of public space from ordinary Washington-area users—who have relied on its affordability and location for generations—to a prestige project dictated from the White House.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

A deadline built around the administration’s timetable

The immediate dispute concerns how quickly Reyes should decide whether the government may keep part of East Potomac Park closed. Her temporary restraining order keeps the park open but excludes the golf course, leaving the administration’s central objective largely intact while the litigation proceeds. Over the weekend, the course gave away its training clubs, photographer Andrew Leyden reported, a practical sign that the shutdown was already being treated as more than a temporary interruption.

The administration argues that witness testimony and extended proceedings would waste time. Its preferred schedule would close written arguments before Thanksgiving and permit Reyes to rule before the restraining order lapses.

The plaintiffs want time to investigate. They are seeking testimony from contractors to compare what those parties were told with representations made by the Justice Department and White House. They also argue that the government’s compressed schedule would disrupt witnesses’ plans during the holiday week.

That procedural disagreement carries the substance of the case. The administration wants the judge to decide rapidly on the existing record; its opponents want to test how that record was constructed. Speed, under those circumstances, is not neutral. It benefits the institution that made the decision, terminated the existing operation and began defending the resulting closure.

Safety appeared after Trump’s directive

The administration has said the island needed to close because its seawall was submerged or collapsing. But according to AlterNet’s account, safety was not part of the government’s stated case until after Trump announced on Truth Social that the course would close Nov. 15 for redevelopment into a championship-level venue.

That chronology is why further testimony matters. The allegation is not simply that officials offered an unpersuasive explanation. The Justice Department has been accused of inventing a justification that would allow renovation work to begin without the required approval. Government lawyers dispute the court’s earlier finding that they acted in bad faith.

Reyes has already identified a more direct chain of responsibility. In her temporary restraining order, she found that the Park Service ended the existing operator’s role “so that it could close the Park to effectuate President Trump’s directive to begin work on the Fazio Design immediately.” She also rejected the notion that the absence of an operator was an independent problem confronting the government: federal officials had created that condition themselves.

The distinction is crucial. Bureaucracies often present the consequences of their own decisions as external constraints—there is no operator, the facility cannot function, closure is unavoidable. Reyes’s finding cuts through that misdirection. The Park Service removed the operator in service of the president’s redevelopment order and then faced the operational vacuum its decision produced.

A public course converted into a presidential project

The institutional power here is not held by the local golfers, runners or cyclists who use East Potomac Park. It belongs to the president who issued the directive, the Park Service that acted on it and the Justice Department now pressing the court to resolve the challenge before opponents can gather the testimony they say they need.

The proposed transformation also reveals whose interests count in the redevelopment. The existing course’s political value lies precisely in features a prestige project can erase: it is affordable, accessible and embedded in a larger public park. Trump’s plan would turn the entire island into a tournament-scale venue. The promised upgrade therefore carries a concrete loss, replacing broad everyday use with a facility designed around championship status and official events.

Whether the administration’s safety claims withstand scrutiny remains a matter for the court. But the reported sequence is already clear: Trump announced the closure and redevelopment; safety concerns entered the government’s explanation afterward; the Park Service terminated the operator; and the Justice Department now seeks a ruling without the evidentiary hearing opponents want. The government is asking the court to treat urgency as a reason to curtail scrutiny when that urgency arose from the government’s own rush to execute the president’s order.

item.title: Leaker reveals how Trump 'deliberately' gutted essential US cyber defenses
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Miles Taylor, a former senior Homeland Security official in Donald Trump’s first administration, says the president has systematically weakened the federal government’s ability to defend essential infrastructure from cyberattack. His warning rests on two reported decisions: the Trump administration loosened oversight of artificial intelligence systems that can be weaponized against digital infrastructure, and after returning to office in 2025, it hollowed out the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure
item.content:encoded:
Miles Taylor, a former senior Homeland Security official in Donald Trump’s first administration, says the president has systematically weakened the federal government’s ability to defend essential infrastructure from cyberattack. His warning rests on two reported decisions: the Trump administration loosened oversight of artificial intelligence systems that can be weaponized against digital infrastructure, and after returning to office in 2025, it hollowed out the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency just as AI was making cyber threats more dangerous.

Taylor’s assessment is not an official finding or a prediction with a fixed timetable. But the institutional damage he describes is concrete: CISA has lost roughly one-third of its workforce, remains without a Senate-confirmed director, and faces a proposed $700 million cut. The people with the power to reverse that deterioration are not hackers, civil servants or frightened consumers. They are the president and the officials carrying out his agenda.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

An agency punished after contradicting Trump

Taylor helped draft the law that created CISA and later watched Trump sign it. Congress designed the agency to serve as the federal government’s principal domestic cyber-defense operation, protecting the systems that keep elections, communications, transportation and commerce functioning.

The agency’s political trouble began when it performed that mission in a way Trump found personally inconvenient. After the 2020 election, CISA’s first director rejected Trump’s false narrative that the election had been stolen and described it as the most secure in US history. Trump fired him by tweet.

That sequence matters. The dispute was not over whether CISA had failed to protect the election. The agency’s offense was contradicting the president’s preferred account of an election he lost. Taylor says Trump subsequently dismantled the programs built to defend the country, then “shredded the agency” after returning to power in 2025.

This is institutional retaliation with a public cost. A cyber-defense agency cannot function as intended if its leaders and employees understand that accurate assessments may be punished whenever they collide with presidential claims. Weakening its staff and leadership compounds that pressure: it reduces both the agency’s technical capacity and its ability to speak with authority inside the government.

Technical capacity traded for political obedience

Current and former CISA employees told Taylor that the agency is now “a shell of its former self.” One described a threadbare staff, with only a small number of employees able to understand advanced AI developments, and said the White House would not listen even if the agency tried to act.

That account exposes the practical consequence of governing through loyalty tests. Cybersecurity depends on specialized expertise, sustained preparation and officials willing to report unwelcome facts. Trump’s treatment of CISA, as Taylor describes it, has degraded all three.

The administration’s approach to AI adds another layer of exposure. Taylor argues that Trump gave the industry a “hall pass” by removing safety rules and permitting reckless deployment. He attributes that policy to the influence of technology executives who cultivated Trump through money and flattery and were rewarded with diminished oversight.

The source material does not identify the particular regulations, executives or transactions behind that characterization, so it does not establish a specific quid pro quo. The documented political structure is nevertheless clear: the administration controls federal safeguards, industry stands to benefit from their removal, and the public bears the risk when powerful systems are deployed without adequate defenses.

A warning, not proof of a particular attack

AlterNet notes that aviation, communications, banking and commercial systems had suffered major problems during the preceding week, with cyberattackers blamed for some of them. The reporting does not establish that every disruption was a cyberattack, that AI caused the incidents, or that CISA’s reduced capacity allowed them to occur.

Taylor’s broader warning is prospective. He says Americans may not grasp the weakness of federal defenses until attacks produce rolling outages, block access to cash, disrupt travel and public services, create shortages or shut down electricity. Those are scenarios, not reported outcomes. His claim is that an administration responsible for preparing against them has made preparedness substantially worse.

He compares the government’s vulnerability to the failures preceding the September 11 attacks, calling the present lack of readiness “vastly worse.” That is an extraordinary assessment from a former official, but it remains his assessment. The staffing losses, leadership vacuum and proposed budget reduction give it more substance than a generic warning, even if they cannot establish when an attack will occur or how severe it would be.

“On our own” is a consequence of government policy

Former Trump White House press secretary Stephanie Grisham wrote that she no longer believed or trusted the people running the government. Taylor went further, warning against accepting assurances from the White House or Homeland Security that the threat is under control.

Personal distrust from former officials is not itself evidence of an imminent cyberattack. The sharper indictment lies in what Taylor reports about the machinery of government: an agency created to protect the public contradicted Trump, its leader was fired, and its workforce and authority were then diminished during a period of escalating technical risk.

Taylor says Americans are more “on our own” than they realize. If that is now true, it is not because cybersecurity somehow became too complicated for government. It is because officials with the authority to maintain the country’s defenses chose to strip capacity from the institution built for the job.
