item.title: Trump relative exposes 'dark family tradition' behind his major corruption
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Mary Trump says her uncle’s willingness to accept valuable gifts, including benefits she characterizes as bribes, reflects a family rule taught across generations: never turn down money. Her account offers a revealing picture of the values cultivated inside the Trump family. It does not, by itself, establish the cause of any specific act of presidential corruption—and it does not reduce Donald Trump’s responsibility for choices made while holding the power of the presidency. That distinction mat
item.content:encoded:
Mary Trump says her uncle’s willingness to accept valuable gifts, including benefits she characterizes as bribes, reflects a family rule taught across generations: never turn down money. Her account offers a revealing picture of the values cultivated inside the Trump family. It does not, by itself, establish the cause of any specific act of presidential corruption—and it does not reduce Donald Trump’s responsibility for choices made while holding the power of the presidency.

That distinction matters. A family history can explain how entitlement becomes ordinary. It cannot convert an officeholder’s conduct into an inherited reflex for which nobody is accountable.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Money as the family’s measure of value

In a video described by AlterNet, Mary Trump said money was “the only currency” that mattered in her family. The psychologist and daughter of Donald Trump’s late older brother, Fred Trump Jr., attributed that culture to her grandfather, Fred Trump Sr., whom she called “a straight-up sociopath.”

Her clearest evidence is a lesson from her grandmother, Mary Anne MacLeod Trump. While Mary Trump was a graduate student at Columbia University, her apartment was burglarized. Among the stolen belongings was the electric typewriter she needed for her dissertation. Her grandmother offered her a check for a replacement, but she declined, saying she would manage on her own.

The response was blunt: “Mary, never reject a gift of money.”

Mary Trump presented that advice as more than one grandmother’s practical reaction to a burglary. She said the principle had been instilled in Donald Trump and much of the wider family for years.

She also recalled that her grandparents sent family members two checks at Christmas. The sums were not life-changing, she said, but neither were they trivial. In her telling, the checks became part of a family order in which money was not merely useful; accepting it was treated as self-evidently correct.

The relative who returned the checks

Another episode shows what happened when someone refused that order. Mary Trump said the wives of her uncles Donald and Robert sought to exclude her mother from family holiday gatherings. Offended by the decision, her mother returned the gift checks she continued to receive.

Other family members could not understand the gesture, according to Mary Trump. Her mother had treated the money as subordinate to dignity and relationship. In a family culture organized around accepting financial benefit, returning it apparently registered less as a moral protest than as an incomprehensible rejection of value itself.

That anecdote is politically relevant because public corruption depends on a similar collapse of distinctions. A gift is not harmless merely because someone is willing to give it. Its meaning depends on who provides it, who receives it, what access or influence accompanies it, and what public authority the recipient controls.

But Mary Trump’s family memories are evidence of a culture, not proof that this culture produced any particular presidential act. AlterNet’s framing outruns the material it presents: the article invokes Donald Trump’s “endless corruption” and acceptance of bribes without identifying a specific transaction, finding, or adjudicated case. The reported substance is Mary Trump’s psychological and familial interpretation.

Explanation is not exoneration

Mary Trump did not use upbringing to excuse her uncle. “Can we blame Donald for accepting gifts of value even if they’re actually bribes? Yes. Yes, we can,” she said.

That is the essential point. Donald Trump did not choose what his parents taught him, but he chooses how he exercises institutional power. A president has obligations that do not disappear because acquisitiveness was normalized at home. Indeed, high office makes the distinction between a gift and a corrupt inducement more important, because the recipient possesses authority over policy, enforcement, appointments, contracts and access.

Family pathology can become a convenient form of misdirection when it turns a powerful adult’s conduct into the inevitable residue of childhood. It relocates agency from the officeholder to dead parents and inherited dysfunction. Mary Trump’s account is most useful when read more narrowly: it describes an environment that may have trained family members to see refusing money as irrational. It does not establish motive in any individual case, and it does not transfer responsibility away from the person accepting the benefit.

Her proposed remedy was to teach children better values and require leaders to reject monetary gifts. The first is family counsel. The second is a question of public power and enforceable limits. Ethical government cannot depend on whether an officeholder received sound advice from a grandmother. It requires rules strong enough to constrain leaders who learned exactly the opposite.

item.title: NYT columnist warns the death of the Electoral College far from certain
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: The Electoral College is not nearing extinction merely because Democratic state governments could, in theory, assemble enough electoral votes to route around it. New York Times columnist Jamelle Bouie’s warning is more concrete: the proposed workaround depends on partisan officials honoring an adverse result and a Republican-dominated Supreme Court permitting an untested compact to operate. Neither outcome is assured. AlterNet reports that recent midterm elections produced enough new Democratic
item.content:encoded:
The Electoral College is not nearing extinction merely because Democratic state governments could, in theory, assemble enough electoral votes to route around it. New York Times columnist Jamelle Bouie’s warning is more concrete: the proposed workaround depends on partisan officials honoring an adverse result and a Republican-dominated Supreme Court permitting an untested compact to operate. Neither outcome is assured.

AlterNet reports that recent midterm elections produced enough new Democratic state-government trifectas to reach the compact’s decisive 270-vote threshold if those states join. That is an opening, not a victory. The Constitution’s presidential machinery would remain intact, along with the officials and judges empowered to determine whether the workaround survives its first serious test.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

A popular vote assembled state by state

The National Popular Vote Interstate Compact would require participating states to award their electoral votes to the candidate who wins the most votes nationwide. It would take effect only after member states collectively control at least 270 electoral votes—the number required to win the presidency.

If implemented and enforced, the compact would make the national popular-vote winner president without formally abolishing the Electoral College. States would use their existing authority over the appointment of electors to neutralize the system’s capacity to elevate the second-place candidate.

That capacity has twice determined the presidency in recent decades. George W. Bush won in 2000 without winning the national popular vote, and Donald Trump did the same in 2016. Those outcomes sharpened opposition to a system that gives voters different practical weight depending on where they live.

But describing the compact as a means of “ending” the Electoral College overstates what it would do. It would leave the institution standing and attempt to redirect its operation through coordinated state law. That distinction matters because every unresolved legal and political vulnerability remains available to opponents.

The compact’s first test would be partisan

Bouie doubts that state governments will reliably surrender their electoral votes when the national result favors the opposing party.

“I’m skeptical that if a Republican wins the popular vote, Democratic states will want to give up their Electoral College votes and vice versa,” he said in a YouTube video.

That is not a minor implementation concern. It goes to the compact’s governing premise: that state officials will accept losing power under rules they endorsed when the result was hypothetical. A national popular-vote system established by constitutional amendment would bind every state under one explicit rule. The compact instead relies on a collection of state governments maintaining their commitments under maximum partisan pressure.

The political temptation is obvious. A state legislature could face a result in which its own voters decisively support one candidate while the national electorate chooses another. The compact requires that state to assign its electors against the preference expressed within its borders. Whether lawmakers would attempt to withdraw, revise the law or otherwise obstruct that outcome has not been tested in a presidential election.

Bouie’s skepticism applies across party lines. That is not “both sides” absolution; it identifies where authority sits. Voters do not administer the compact. State officials do, and those officials would confront powerful incentives to preserve an electoral advantage for their party.

The Supreme Court remains a veto point

Even if participating states honor the agreement, litigation would be virtually certain. Bouie said there is an open constitutional question about whether states may use a compact to accomplish indirectly what would otherwise require changing the Constitution.

“It’s never been tried before,” he said. “And I have a feeling that Republicans on the Supreme Court may not go for it.”

The compact’s supporters may be able to assemble 270 electoral votes on paper, but the Supreme Court holds the institutional power to decide whether that arrangement survives. A strategy built around state authority therefore runs directly toward a federal judiciary whose Republican-appointed majority may reject it.

This is the central weakness obscured by celebratory arithmetic. Adding electoral votes tells readers when the compact could activate. It does not establish that the compact would be obeyed, enforced or upheld. The votes needed to trigger a legal mechanism are not the same as the power needed to protect it.

A compromise born of exhaustion and self-interest

Bouie also rejects the ceremonial mythology surrounding the Electoral College. He described it not as a carefully engineered achievement but as a “kludge” produced by practical limitations, distrust of mass democracy and political bargaining.

The framers faced technological and logistical obstacles to conducting a national popular vote, he said. Some also distrusted direct democratic participation. Southern delegates had an additional material interest: securing presidential influence from enslaved populations who were denied any political voice.

That history strips away the institution’s borrowed prestige. Longevity does not prove coherent design, and constitutional origin does not erase the interests embedded in a compromise. Bouie argued that the system “basically stopped working after George Washington declined to stand for a third term,” when organized partisan competition exposed assumptions that had not survived the nation’s first presidency.

The compact is an attempt to repair that inherited arrangement without securing the constitutional amendment required to replace it outright. Its growing numerical viability is politically significant. But the decisive struggle begins after the spreadsheet reaches 270: when state officials must accept a result they dislike and the Supreme Court must decide whether voters may obtain majority rule through a mechanism the Constitution never expressly designed.

item.title: The Forbidden Book: How Religion Learned to Fear Its Own Scriptures
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: For centuries, religious authorities claimed to possess humanity’s ultimate truth. Their problem was that people might actually read it. There is a peculiar irony in the history of Western civilization: the institution that claimed to possess the ultimate source of truth spent considerable portions of its history deciding who was allowed to read it, what they were permitted to understand, and which questions they were forbidden to ask. Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself
item.content:encoded:
For centuries, religious authorities claimed to possess humanity’s ultimate truth. Their problem was that people might actually read it.

There is a peculiar irony in the history of Western civilization: the institution that claimed to possess the ultimate source of truth spent considerable portions of its history deciding who was allowed to read it, what they were permitted to understand, and which questions they were forbidden to ask.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

And it wasn't just any institution.

It was the Church.

The same institution that proclaimed the Bible to be the divinely inspired word of an omniscient, omnipotent, and infinitely benevolent God.

Apparently, this perfect divine revelation was too dangerous to leave in the hands of ordinary people.

I recently watched a YouTube video titled Why Did Human Progress COLLAPSE in Western Europe?. It traces the decline of the Western Roman Empire, the fragmentation of its sophisticated economic and educational systems, and the subsequent concentration of intellectual authority within the medieval Church.

Its central argument is provocative: the collapse of Rome destroyed the infrastructure that supported widespread learning, and the Church, which inherited much of what remained, became a gatekeeper of knowledge.

The video takes considerable liberties with historical complexity. Medieval Europe wasn't intellectually frozen for a thousand years, and Christianity wasn't solely responsible for the continent's difficulties. Monasteries preserved classical manuscripts, church-sponsored universities became centers of learning, and medieval scholars made genuine advances in mathematics, philosophy, architecture, and natural science.

But correcting those exaggerations doesn't erase the institutional abuses that really happened.

The video raises a much more important question than whether Christianity single-handedly caused the so-called Dark Ages.

What happens when an institution claims the authority to decide what humanity is allowed to know?

And, perhaps more embarrassingly for Christianity:

What happens when people are finally allowed to read the book that supposedly justifies that authority?

The Church Didn't Invent Ignorance. It Learned to Govern It.

When the Western Roman Empire disintegrated, it took enormous parts of its economic and administrative infrastructure with it.

Roads deteriorated. Cities contracted. Trade networks fragmented. The financial and institutional systems supporting specialized professions, education, and large public works weakened or disappeared in many regions.

The damage was neither immediate nor uniform, and the Eastern Roman Empire continued for centuries. Nevertheless, significant parts of Western Europe experienced a profound loss of economic and institutional complexity.

The Church survived much of this fragmentation.

Its bishops, monasteries, administrative networks, and shared written language provided continuity when other institutions failed.

That continuity was genuinely valuable. Without medieval scribes, many ancient texts might not have survived.

But preservation and control can exist in the same institution.

When an organization becomes one of the principal custodians of books, schools, and literacy, it gains extraordinary influence over which texts circulate and how they are interpreted.

And when that organization believes its religious doctrines are divinely guaranteed, intellectual disagreement can become something far more serious than an academic dispute.

It can become heresy.

Around 601 CE, Pope Gregory the Great reprimanded Bishop Desiderius of Vienne over reports that he was teaching classical grammar and literature. Gregory objected to the celebration of pagan authors by a Christian bishop, arguing that the praises of Christ and Jupiter did not belong together.

This was not a universal prohibition on classical education. Gregory himself recognized uses for secular learning.

But the episode illustrates a revealing institutional priority: knowledge could be acceptable or unacceptable depending on its perceived compatibility with religious obligations.

That principle becomes dangerous when the institution applying it also possesses the power to punish dissent.

A mistaken scientific theory can be corrected by evidence.

A mistaken scientific theory declared to be religious truth is considerably harder to dislodge.

The problem is no longer merely determining what is true.

It is determining who has permission to challenge what powerful people insist is true.

The Bible: Too Sacred for Ordinary People to Read

Here is where the history becomes almost comically self-defeating.

The Bible was supposed to contain God's message to humanity.

Not merely advice. Not an interesting collection of ancient literature. Not the philosophical speculations of fallible men.

God's own revelation.

You might reasonably expect an institution making that claim to want every human being to read it.

Preferably in a language they understood.

Yet in certain periods and regions, Church authorities did precisely the opposite.

In 1229, the Synod of Toulouse imposed restrictions on laypeople possessing biblical books, particularly versions in local languages. Similar restrictions followed in Tarragona. In England, the Constitutions of Oxford in 1408 restricted unauthorized English translations and the reading of unapproved versions.

These were not universal prohibitions on every vernacular Bible throughout Christian history. Some translations circulated with ecclesiastical approval, and the restrictions varied substantially across time and place.

The authorities also had specific concerns about movements they considered heretical, unauthorized interpretations, and the reliability of translations.

But the central issue remains.

The institution that declared scripture essential to spiritual salvation could, under particular circumstances, punish people for possessing or reading it without authorization.

Think about the implications.

If a book contains an infallible moral truth intended for all humanity, why should understanding it require the approval of an institutional intermediary?

And if an interpretation of scripture is demonstrably correct, why should independent reading threaten it?

There is a perfectly straightforward answer.

Controlling the interpretation of a sacred text is a form of power.

The problem with an independently literate population is not necessarily that people will abandon religion.

It is that they might no longer require the people who claim exclusive authority to explain it.

Nothing Makes an Atheist Faster Than Reading the Bible

There is an old joke among atheists that the surest way to create another atheist is to encourage someone to read the Bible from cover to cover.

It is a joke, not a universal psychological law.

Millions of people have read the Bible carefully and remained devout believers. Many have devoted their lives to its study.

But the joke contains an uncomfortable observation.

The Bible is often considerably more troubling than the sanitized version of it presented in sermons, Sunday schools, and inspirational social media posts.

Consider a few passages.

In 1 Samuel 15:3, God instructs Saul to destroy the Amalekites, including men, women, children, infants, and livestock.

Not merely defeat an opposing army.

Exterminate an entire population.

In Numbers 31, Moses commands the killing of Midianite boys and women who have had sexual relations, while permitting the young virgin girls to be kept alive.

In Exodus 21, the biblical law regulates slavery, including conditions under which people can be purchased, held, and subjected to physical punishment.

It does not simply announce that owning another human being is morally unacceptable.

In Deuteronomy 22:28–29, a man who seizes and has intercourse with an unbetrothed virgin must pay her father and marry her, with no subsequent right of divorce. Scholars debate whether the Hebrew describes rape in the same sense as another passage in the chapter, but the law's treatment of the woman as subject to a compulsory marriage arrangement is disturbing regardless.

And in 2 Kings 2:23–24, after youths mock the prophet Elisha, two bears emerge and maul forty-two of them following his curse.

These passages exist in the same collection of writings that believers are routinely told reveals a perfectly loving and just deity.

Naturally, religious apologists have explanations.

The Amalekites were supposedly exceptionally wicked.

The killing of children was part of divine judgment.

Slavery was an accommodation to ancient social conditions.

The troubling laws must be interpreted in historical context.

The massacre narratives might be hyperbolic.

And the bears? Well, apparently mocking a prophet was a considerably more serious offense than modern readers might expect.

Some of these arguments raise legitimate historical and literary considerations. Ancient Near Eastern warfare narratives did employ exaggerated language, biblical books reflect different genres and historical settings, and religious traditions have developed sophisticated interpretive frameworks.

But historical explanation is not the same as moral justification.

We can understand why ancient societies practiced slavery without concluding that slavery was acceptable.

We can understand the conventions of ancient warfare without accepting genocide as an expression of perfect justice.

And we can examine an ancient culture's moral assumptions without pretending they came from an omniscient being who possessed timeless knowledge of right and wrong.

Which brings us to the problem that theological explanations so often fail to resolve.

Who Is Correcting Whom?

Modern Christians generally reject slavery.

Most reject genocide.

Most would be horrified by a government executing children for the crimes of their parents.

Many reject the rigid subordination of women found in portions of biblical literature.

And that is a good thing.

But it introduces a philosophical difficulty.

If scripture contains timeless moral guidance from a morally perfect deity, why do modern believers repeatedly need to reinterpret, qualify, or reject what earlier generations understood it to authorize?

Why does contemporary morality so often require us to explain why the apparent meaning of a biblical passage should not be followed?

Consider slavery.

Human beings eventually developed compelling moral arguments against the institution, culminating in abolitionist movements that included both religious and secular advocates.

Some Christians fought slavery because of their faith.

Other Christians defended slavery using the same Bible.

The text was available to both.

Their conclusions were radically different.

The decisive issue was not simply who possessed scripture.

It was which moral principles they brought to its interpretation.

And that reveals an uncomfortable possibility:

Perhaps we are not deriving our morality from scripture. Perhaps we are using our morality to decide which parts of scripture deserve our approval.

When a modern believer rejects biblical slavery because it violates human dignity, I agree with the believer.

But I would argue that the recognition of human dignity is doing the ethical work.

The biblical text is being judged against a standard the reader already considers important.

And if human reasoning and empathy can determine that a biblical instruction is morally unacceptable, then human reasoning and empathy have demonstrated an independence from the claimed authority of that instruction.

We don't need to prove that every religious person is immoral, or that religion has never inspired moral progress.

Neither proposition is true.

We need only recognize that claiming divine authority does not establish moral correctness.

When Reality Contradicts Revelation

The video moves from the preservation and control of knowledge to another notorious chapter in religious history: the suppression of scientific ideas.

Its examples include Galileo Galilei, Giordano Bruno, and the Church's prohibitions against certain philosophical and astronomical propositions.

Here, too, historical accuracy matters.

Bruno was not executed simply because he believed stars were other suns. His condemnation involved multiple theological propositions considered heretical.

Galileo's conflict with the Catholic Church was entangled with scriptural interpretation, academic disputes, and ecclesiastical politics.

But these qualifications do not absolve the institution.

Galileo was tried by the Roman Inquisition in 1633, compelled to abjure heliocentrism, and placed under house arrest.

He was punished by religious authorities for defending a proposition concerning the physical universe.

And the Earth continued orbiting the Sun.

This is the fundamental problem with granting theological institutions authority over empirical questions.

The universe has no obligation to conform to doctrine.

Planets do not alter their trajectories because a bishop disapproves.

Diseases do not change their mechanisms to accommodate scripture.

And reality does not become less real because somebody declares it heretical.

Science, when functioning properly, possesses an essential advantage over dogmatic authority.

Its conclusions can be challenged.

An established theory can be overturned by sufficiently strong evidence.

A researcher does not need to establish that a competing explanation is spiritually acceptable. The explanation must survive observation, experimentation, and criticism.

Scientific institutions are themselves imperfect. Researchers have prejudices. Academic hierarchies resist disruptive ideas. Fraud occurs. Entire communities can become invested in mistaken theories.

But those are failures of human institutions, not necessary requirements of scientific reasoning.

A scientific conclusion remains open to correction.

By contrast, when an institution declares a proposition infallible, it creates a profound incentive to defend that proposition regardless of what new evidence appears.

The scientist asks what the evidence demonstrates.

The dogmatist asks whether the evidence is permitted to be correct.

Only one of those questions is capable of reliably advancing human knowledge.

The Church Eventually Made Its Position Explicit

In 1864, Pope Pius IX published the Syllabus of Errors, a collection of eighty propositions the Catholic Church condemned.

The final proposition rejected the claim that the Roman Pontiff could and should reconcile himself with progress, liberalism, and modern civilization.

The precise theological and political context matters. This was not a blanket declaration that every technological advance was evil. It concerned the Church's confrontation with particular modern political and philosophical developments, including liberalism and the changing relationship between religious and civil authority.

Nevertheless, the choice of language is extraordinary.

An institution claiming to represent eternal truth had placed itself in explicit opposition to major currents of modern political and intellectual development.

There is something almost admirable about the clarity.

No elaborate public-relations campaign.

No carefully worded statement about respectful dialogue.

Just an official rejection of a proposition calling for reconciliation with modern civilization.

And this wasn't an obscure medieval council operating in an age when most Europeans could not read.

It was 1864.

The Industrial Revolution was transforming economies.

Charles Darwin had published On the Origin of Species five years earlier.

Modern scientific institutions were expanding.

And the papacy was still formally condemning propositions it associated with modern liberalism.

This is not evidence that every religious believer opposed progress.

It is evidence that religious institutions could perceive changes in political authority, intellectual freedom, and social organization as threats to their own position.

Which is precisely why institutions claiming infallible authority should never be exempt from scrutiny.

The Printing Press Did Something Far More Dangerous Than Print Books

The video's account gives Johannes Gutenberg and the spread of printing a central role in breaking the institutional concentration of written knowledge.

There is good reason for that.

The printing press dramatically reduced the cost of reproducing texts and accelerated their circulation.

A manuscript could be confiscated.

A printing operation could produce hundreds or thousands of copies.

A forbidden idea could cross a border faster than the authorities could suppress it.

Printing did not immediately produce intellectual freedom. Both Catholic and Protestant authorities practiced censorship, and the technology could distribute propaganda, prejudice, and falsehoods just as efficiently as scientific discoveries.

But the technology changed the economics of controlling information.

Martin Luther's writings spread through print networks.

Bible translations became more accessible.

Competing theological interpretations proliferated.

And ordinary readers acquired opportunities to encounter arguments without depending entirely on a local religious authority.

The consequences were not uniformly peaceful or enlightened. The Reformation helped unleash generations of religious conflict and persecution.

But the institutional monopoly on interpretation was being challenged.

And the principle extended well beyond religion.

Once information can circulate independently of the institution claiming to control it, authority has to compete with inquiry.

It can no longer rely exclusively on controlling the available texts.

It must contend with readers.

And readers are notoriously inconvenient.

They compare passages.

They notice contradictions.

They ask why one instruction is literal while another is metaphorical.

They wonder why an eternal moral truth appears to change whenever society develops a better understanding of justice.

Sometimes they remain religious.

Sometimes they change denominations.

Sometimes they reconstruct their beliefs.

And sometimes they become atheists.

Not because someone prohibited them from believing.

But because they were finally free to examine what they had been told to believe.

Atheism Doesn't Require the Bible to Be Entirely Wrong

There is another distinction worth making.

The Bible contains historically valuable material, poetry, philosophy, ancient law, religious reflection, and narratives that have shaped civilizations.

Some of its moral teachings are admirable.

Others are horrifying.

Still others are products of historical circumstances that no longer exist.

None of these observations requires dismissing the entire collection as worthless.

A text can possess enormous literary, cultural, and historical importance without being divinely inspired.

The Iliad remains a masterpiece without requiring us to believe Athena intervened on the battlefield.

The Epic of Gilgamesh remains profoundly meaningful without establishing the historical existence of its gods.

And the Bible can be studied seriously without treating every theological claim contained within it as an accurate description of reality.

In fact, removing the demand that scripture be infallible can make its study more intellectually productive.

We can examine contradictions without inventing harmonizations.

We can acknowledge that biblical authors reflected different theological perspectives.

We can identify moral failures without pretending they were secretly virtues.

We can appreciate the humanity of ancient writers without attributing their prejudices to a perfect divine intelligence.

The Bible becomes what it demonstrably is: an extraordinarily influential collection of ancient religious literature.

That does not establish that no god exists.

But it removes the assumption that the Bible must be correct because religious authorities say it is.

And once that assumption disappears, the claims of revelation must stand on their own evidence.

The Real Threat Was Never the Book

This brings us back to the original historical irony.

Why would religious authorities restrict access to scripture?

The documented motivations varied. There were concerns about heresy, translation accuracy, unauthorized preaching, and maintaining doctrinal unity.

It would be historically irresponsible to claim that medieval Church leaders banned vernacular Bibles because they feared creating atheists.

That is our joke, not their documented explanation.

But the joke highlights something their policies reveal.

An institution that claims to possess ultimate truth may still fear losing control over how that truth is interpreted.

And once maintaining authority becomes a priority, independent inquiry becomes a problem to manage.

The same mechanism can appear in political ideologies, authoritarian governments, and secular institutions.

It is not uniquely religious.

But religion introduces an especially powerful justification: divine authority.

A political leader can claim to be wise.

A religious leader can claim that disagreement constitutes defiance of God.

That changes the stakes considerably.

An argument over evidence becomes an argument over obedience.

A competing interpretation becomes heresy.

A challenge to institutional authority becomes a threat to spiritual salvation.

And when those claims are backed by state power, the consequences can become lethal.

History provides enough examples without requiring us to invent additional ones.

The Door Must Remain Open

The video ends with an observation that deserves to survive even after we strip away its exaggerated historical narrative.

Human progress is not inevitable.

Civilizations can lose knowledge.

Institutions can suppress inquiry.

Economic collapse can destroy educational systems.

Governments can censor information.

Religious authorities can punish dissent.

And entire societies can convince themselves that protecting established beliefs is more important than discovering whether those beliefs are true.

The lesson is not that religious people are incapable of scientific reasoning.

History decisively disproves that.

Nor is it that atheists are inherently immune to dogma.

They aren't.

The lesson is that no institution, religious or secular, deserves immunity from evidence, criticism, or moral scrutiny.

No proposition becomes true because an authority declares it sacred.

No moral instruction becomes good simply because someone attributes it to a deity.

And no book becomes infallible because generations of people have been taught never to question it.

Which brings us back to that old atheist joke.

Perhaps reading the Bible won't make someone an atheist.

Perhaps it will strengthen their faith.

Perhaps it will lead them to a different understanding of religion.

Or perhaps it will make them confront questions their religious teachers never mentioned.

But that is precisely the point.

The outcome of an honest investigation cannot be prescribed in advance.

If a belief is true, it should be able to withstand examination.

If a moral principle is sound, it should survive criticism.

And if an institution claims to possess the ultimate truth, it should welcome the most rigorous scrutiny imaginable.

Because truth doesn't need protection from questions.

Authority frequently does.

And if there's one thing the history of forbidden books teaches us, it's this:

The most dangerous thing you can give someone who has been taught what to think is the freedom to read, reason, and decide for themselves.

Sources and further reading

  • Why Did Human Progress COLLAPSE in Western Europe? — YouTube. The video's historical narrative and central arguments are the starting point for this essay.

  • David C. Lindberg and Michael H. Shank, “Science and the Medieval Church,” The Cambridge History of Science. A scholarly treatment of medieval Christianity's complicated relationship with scientific learning.

  • Pope Gregory the Great, Letter to Desiderius. A primary-source example of ecclesiastical concern about classical education.

  • New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge, “Bible Reading by the Laity, Restrictions on”. Historical documentation of restrictions on vernacular scripture.

  • Catholic Encyclopedia, “Scripture”. A Catholic account of the scope and context of medieval Bible restrictions.

  • Pope Pius IX, Syllabus of Errors (1864). The original document, including its eightieth condemned proposition.

item.title: Private Equity: When Destroying a Company Becomes a Business Model
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos

item.content:encoded:
Wall Street calls it investment. Workers call it unemployment. Creditors call it bankruptcy. And the people who engineered the deal may have already collected their fees.

There is something profoundly disturbing about a financial system in which someone can buy a successful business, saddle it with debt, extract millions of dollars, sell off its assets, and walk away while the company collapses.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Even more disturbing is that much of this can be perfectly legal.

Welcome to the world of private equity, where the distinction between creating wealth and extracting it has become increasingly difficult to ignore.

Over the past three decades, private equity firms have acquired thousands of American businesses. Some acquisitions have produced genuine improvements. Others have ended in bankruptcies, shuttered stores, lost jobs, devastated retirement savings, and communities stripped of institutions that once served them.

And while the companies themselves may disappear, the financial managers who controlled them don't necessarily leave empty-handed.

The question isn't whether private equity can make money.

Clearly, it can.

The question is whether making money should be considered a successful investment when the business generating that money is left in ruins.

The Art of Buying Something With Someone Else's Money

To understand the problem, we need to understand a financial mechanism called the leveraged buyout, or LBO.

Imagine a company that has been operating profitably for decades. It employs thousands of people, owns valuable real estate, maintains relationships with suppliers, and generates dependable revenue.

A private equity firm wants to buy it.

But rather than paying the entire purchase price with its own money, the firm finances a substantial portion of the acquisition through borrowing.

Nothing inherently unusual there. Businesses borrow money all the time.

The interesting part comes afterward.

In a typical leveraged buyout, the acquired company's assets and future cash flows help secure or service the acquisition debt. The business effectively becomes responsible for financing a substantial portion of the transaction that transferred its ownership.

Now the company must generate enough money not only to operate but also to service obligations arising from its own acquisition.

And the new owners have additional ways to collect money.

They may charge management or advisory fees. They may sell company-owned real estate and lease it back. They may arrange additional borrowing to finance shareholder dividends.

These transactions aren't necessarily illegal, and none automatically proves misconduct.

But consider the incentives.

The owners can receive substantial cash distributions while the company takes on additional financial obligations.

If the business prospers, everyone might benefit.

If it fails, employees lose their jobs, suppliers may go unpaid, creditors absorb losses, and communities lose economic activity.

Meanwhile, the owners may already have recovered some or all of their original investment.

The company carries the debt. The workers carry the consequences. The financial managers already have collected their checks.

That's not an inevitable outcome of every leveraged buyout. It's a possibility built into the financial structure.

And that possibility deserves scrutiny.

Thirty Years of Evidence: What Actually Happens?

Criticizing private equity solely through famous bankruptcies would be intellectually lazy.

After all, companies fail for many reasons. Competition changes. Consumer preferences evolve. Technology makes old business models obsolete. Management makes mistakes.

And private equity firms sometimes acquire businesses that are already struggling.

So let's examine the evidence.

One particularly revealing study comes from researchers Brian Ayash and Mahdi Rastad, who examined 484 American public-to-private leveraged buyouts completed between 1980 and 2006.

Their findings were striking.

Approximately 20% of the leveraged-buyout companies experienced bankruptcy within ten years, compared with roughly 2% of comparable companies.

That's approximately ten times the bankruptcy incidence.

Not ten percent higher.

Ten times.

Now, intellectual honesty requires an important qualification: this finding applies to a particular historical sample of leveraged buyouts. It does not mean every private equity acquisition today carries a 20% bankruptcy probability.

Indeed, research from the United Kingdom examining buyouts between 1995 and 2010 found no comparable increase in insolvency after accounting for differences between firms.

The evidence is not uniform across countries, periods, and acquisition structures.

But the American finding raises a serious question.

If certain financial arrangements produce substantially higher bankruptcy rates, why are those arrangements defended primarily by pointing to the returns they generate for investors?

Bankruptcy isn't merely a disappointing number in a financial report.

It can mean thousands of people losing their livelihoods.

And sometimes, bankruptcy is only the final chapter of a much longer story of financial deterioration.

Toys “R” Us: A Company Buried Under Its Own Acquisition

Consider Toys “R” Us.

For generations, the retailer was practically synonymous with childhood in America.

In 2005, Bain Capital, KKR, and Vornado Realty Trust acquired the company in a leveraged buyout valued at approximately $6.6 billion.

The transaction left Toys “R” Us carrying billions in debt.

Over the following years, the company struggled with changing retail conditions, online competition, and the need to modernize its operations.

Those were genuine business challenges.

But its debt made responding to them considerably harder.

By the years preceding bankruptcy, Toys “R” Us was spending hundreds of millions of dollars annually servicing its financial obligations.

Money used to service debt cannot simultaneously be spent modernizing stores, improving logistics, developing technology, or competing with Amazon and Walmart.

In 2017, Toys “R” Us filed for bankruptcy.

In 2018, its U.S. operations were liquidated, costing tens of thousands of workers their jobs.

Was private equity solely responsible for every problem the retailer faced?

No.

But the acquisition debt unquestionably constrained the company's options.

And that's the distinction that matters.

A business can survive difficult market conditions. A heavily indebted business has fewer resources with which to survive them.

Private equity didn't invent competition.

It helped determine how financially equipped Toys “R” Us was to face it.

The Bankruptcy Hall of Fame

Toys “R” Us is hardly the only recognizable name associated with private equity ownership and financial distress.

J.Crew, Payless ShoeSource, Gymboree, and numerous other retailers experienced bankruptcies after leveraged acquisitions or periods of private equity control.

But we should resist the temptation to place every famous corporate collapse into the same category.

RadioShack, for example, was already financially distressed before an investor group acquired much of its business through bankruptcy.

Bed Bath & Beyond was publicly traded before its 2023 bankruptcy; its collapse was not the result of a conventional private equity leveraged buyout.

And TGI Fridays, whose U.S. corporate operator filed for bankruptcy in 2024 under private equity ownership, faced operational challenges that cannot simply be erased from the story.

These distinctions aren't excuses for private equity.

They're necessary if we want to identify which financial practices actually contribute to corporate failure.

The important question isn't merely whether a private equity firm owned a company that went bankrupt.

It's what happened between acquisition and bankruptcy.

How much debt was added?

How much money was distributed to investors?

How much was collected in fees?

Were assets sold?

Did the company retain sufficient resources to maintain its operations?

And, perhaps most importantly, did the financial managers make money even when the investment ultimately failed?

Those are the questions that expose the difference between unsuccessful investment and potentially destructive financial extraction.

The Employees Are Apparently Disposable

The consequences extend well beyond bankruptcy.

Research by Steven Davis and colleagues, examining thousands of U.S. buyouts, found that employment outcomes varied substantially depending on the type of company acquired.

In public-to-private buyouts, employment at target businesses declined by approximately 12% relative to comparable firms over two years.

In buyouts of previously privately held businesses, employment increased by approximately 15% relative to controls.

That distinction is important.

It demonstrates that private equity doesn't produce identical outcomes everywhere.

But it also reveals something uncomfortable about acquisitions of established public companies.

Workers can spend decades building a business, developing expertise, maintaining customer relationships, and contributing to its success.

Then ownership changes.

Suddenly, the institutional knowledge accumulated over those decades becomes an expense to be reduced.

And when employees object, they're frequently reminded of one of America's most celebrated employment arrangements:

At-will employment.

The employer can generally terminate employment without establishing cause, subject to legal protections against discrimination, unlawful retaliation, and other prohibited grounds.

Defenders insist this arrangement works both ways.

The employer can fire you.

You can quit.

Freedom!

Except the consequences are hardly symmetrical.

When a corporation loses an employee, it generally needs to recruit a replacement.

When an employee loses a job, they may lose their income, health insurance, housing security, and ability to support their family.

The legal freedom may be reciprocal.

The economic vulnerability is not.

And when financial restructuring results in mass layoffs, that imbalance becomes impossible to ignore.

The investors get limited liability. The workers get limited security.

Apparently, that's what passes for equality of bargaining power.

When the Product Is Human Survival

If this were exclusively about struggling retail chains, the damage would already warrant serious attention.

But private equity has increasingly expanded into healthcare, nursing homes, hospitals, veterinary medicine, and other services where customers cannot always walk away.

And the research is troubling.

A study published in the Review of Financial Studies examined private equity acquisitions of nursing homes and estimated an approximately 11% increase in short-term mortality among Medicare patients in the studied facilities.

The researchers also identified reductions in staffing and deterioration in certain measures of care.

Think about what that means.

We're no longer discussing whether a toy store can compete with Amazon.

We're discussing elderly patients who depend on professional caregivers for medication, mobility, hygiene, and survival.

Staffing reductions in these environments aren't merely operational adjustments.

They can have life-or-death consequences.

Research published in JAMA has also identified increases in certain hospital-acquired adverse events following private equity acquisitions of hospitals.

These studies don't establish that every private equity-owned healthcare facility provides inferior care.

But they provide evidence that financial ownership structures can affect outcomes far beyond a company's balance sheet.

And that raises a question society cannot afford to ignore:

Should institutions responsible for vulnerable human beings be subjected to financial incentives that reward aggressive cost reduction and short-term extraction?

The answer cannot be determined solely by whether investors receive attractive returns.

Patients are not portfolio assets.

Neither are elderly residents.

Neither are the people entrusted with caring for them.

The Myth That Every Dollar of Profit Represents Value Created

One of the most persistent defenses of private equity is that its profitability demonstrates its economic value.

But that argument confuses financial returns with productive contribution.

There are many ways to make money.

You can invent a product.

Build a factory.

Improve manufacturing efficiency.

Develop better technology.

Expand into underserved markets.

Or you can acquire an existing business, borrow against its assets, extract distributions, and sell it.

All of those activities may generate financial returns.

They do not necessarily generate equivalent economic value.

McKinsey's 2026 private markets research estimated that cheap leverage and rising valuation multiples accounted for a substantial share—approximately 59%—of buyout returns between 2010 and 2022.

That doesn't mean 59% of private equity profits came from exploiting workers or stripping assets.

It does mean that a considerable portion of historical returns was associated with financing conditions and valuation changes rather than purely operational improvements.

And that distinction matters.

An investor who improves a company's productivity has contributed something measurable.

An investor who benefits from cheap borrowing and sells the same company at a higher valuation may have earned money without producing an equivalent improvement in the underlying business.

Financial profit is not automatically evidence of productive achievement.

Sometimes it's evidence of favorable market conditions.

Sometimes it's evidence of superior management.

And sometimes it reflects the successful transfer of value or risk from one group to another.

Treating all three as interchangeable is not economic analysis.

It's marketing.

But What About the Success Stories?

There are genuine private equity successes.

Dollar General, for example, was acquired by KKR and its partners in 2007, returned to public markets in 2009, and continued expanding.

Some acquisitions provide businesses with needed capital, management expertise, and operational improvements.

Others restructure distressed companies that might otherwise fail.

These outcomes matter because they demonstrate that private equity ownership is not inherently synonymous with corporate destruction.

But they also undermine the idea that destructive practices are unavoidable.

If companies can be acquired, improved, and sold profitably without being financially hollowed out, then aggressive extraction is not an economic necessity.

It's a choice.

The existence of successful acquisitions doesn't excuse harmful ones.

It demonstrates that different financial strategies produce different outcomes.

And that gives us a basis for distinguishing legitimate investment from practices that impose excessive risks on others.

The Real Problem: Who Gets Paid, and When?

Perhaps the most revealing feature of private equity is the separation between the financial interests of fund managers, fund investors, acquired companies, and their employees.

These groups are frequently discussed as though they were interchangeable.

They aren't.

Private equity fund managers may collect management fees regardless of whether a particular portfolio company ultimately succeeds.

Fund investors, meanwhile, can lose substantial portions of their investments.

The acquired company may struggle under debt obligations.

Its employees may face layoffs.

Its creditors may suffer losses.

And its customers may experience declining service.

These are different financial positions, with different incentives and different exposures to risk.

That's why a company going bankrupt doesn't necessarily establish that everyone involved in its ownership lost money.

It also doesn't establish that its owners profited.

We need to follow the money.

In particular, we should examine dividend recapitalizations, in which an acquired company borrows additional money to finance distributions to shareholders.

Such transactions can allow investors to recover capital before selling the business.

They can also increase the company's leverage and vulnerability to future downturns.

The critical question is whether those distributions leave the business with adequate financial resources.

Because when owners can extract substantial cash while leaving the company responsible for additional debt, the incentives can become dangerously misaligned.

The people making the decisions may have already received their rewards before the people living with those decisions experience the consequences.

Thirty Years Later, What Have We Learned?

The evidence doesn't support the simplistic claim that every private equity acquisition destroys a healthy company.

It supports something more specific—and more useful.

Certain leveraged acquisitions have exhibited substantially elevated bankruptcy risks.

Some categories of buyouts have produced significant employment reductions.

Private equity ownership in parts of healthcare has been associated with measurable deterioration in patient outcomes.

Financial structures can allow investors and managers to receive substantial payments while acquired businesses assume additional obligations.

And private equity returns have often depended partly on financing conditions and market valuations, not exclusively on creating operational value.

These findings don't establish that the entire industry is fraudulent.

They establish that judging the industry solely by investment returns leaves out consequences that matter to workers, customers, creditors, and communities.

A financial system cannot be adequately evaluated by asking only how much money its most powerful participants earned.

We also need to ask what happened to everyone else.

Should Private Equity Be Illegal?

That question deserves more serious consideration than it usually receives.

Outright prohibition of private equity ownership would encompass very different activities, including investments that genuinely strengthen businesses.

But there is a strong policy case for examining whether certain acquisition practices should be prohibited or substantially restricted.

For example, lawmakers could consider limits on debt-financed distributions that undermine solvency, tighter oversight of related-party fees, stronger recovery mechanisms for improper payouts, and additional safeguards for essential healthcare services.

They could also examine whether controlling owners should face greater financial responsibility when their decisions materially contribute to insolvency.

None of these measures would eliminate ordinary business failure.

Nor should they.

Companies sometimes fail despite responsible management and legitimate investment.

But there is a difference between accepting commercial risk and designing transactions that permit one group to collect financial rewards while transferring disproportionate risks to everyone else.

Limited liability exists to encourage productive investment.

It should not be confused with an unlimited entitlement to externalize the consequences of financial decisions.

The Failure Was Designed

Wall Street has spent decades developing increasingly sophisticated ways to buy, finance, restructure, and sell businesses.

Financial engineering can serve legitimate economic purposes.

But sophistication doesn't automatically make a transaction socially beneficial.

A company isn't merely a collection of assets available for monetization.

It's also an employer, a customer relationship, a supplier network, a source of tax revenue, and sometimes an essential service.

Its financial statements describe only part of its economic significance.

When investors treat those broader relationships as incidental to their returns, the consequences can extend far beyond the balance sheet.

And when a business collapses after its owners have collected substantial fees and distributions, we should examine the transactions that preceded the collapse rather than accepting bankruptcy as an unfortunate accident.

Not every failure is deliberate.

Not every acquisition is destructive.

But neither should every profitable financial transaction be celebrated as evidence of economic success.

The test should be whether the investment created sustainable value—and who bore the costs of producing its returns.

Because making money from a business is not the same thing as making that business better.

And when the rewards can be collected before the consequences arrive, we shouldn't be surprised when the financial incentives encourage decisions that prioritize the former over the latter.

Research and further reading

  • Brian Ayash and Mahdi Rastad, Leveraged Buyouts and Financial Distress (2019). Research on bankruptcy incidence following U.S. public-to-private leveraged buyouts.

  • Steven J. Davis and colleagues, The Economic Effects of Private Equity Buyouts. National Bureau of Economic Research research on employment, productivity, and business outcomes.

  • Atul Gupta and colleagues, Does Private Equity Investment in Healthcare Benefit Patients? Evidence from Nursing Homes. Review of Financial Studies (2024).

  • Changes in Hospital Adverse Events and Patient Outcomes Associated With Private Equity Acquisition. JAMA (2023).

  • McKinsey & Company, Global Private Markets Report 2026. Research on private equity performance and the drivers of investment returns.

  • S&P Global Market Intelligence, reporting on private-equity-backed corporate bankruptcies, 2024–2026.

  • Private Equity Stakeholder Project, research and reporting on private equity involvement in major corporate bankruptcies.

item.title: GOP operatives warn party bigshots not to run in 2028: 'A suicide mission'
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Republican operatives are already treating the 2028 presidential race as a likely loss. Their warning to ambitious candidates is blunt: challenging for the nomination could amount to a “suicide mission” because any nominee would have to defend President Donald Trump’s record, satisfy an unpredictable MAGA loyalty test and somehow persuade voters who just rejected the party in the 2026 midterms. item.content:encoded:
Republican operatives are already treating the 2028 presidential race as a likely loss. Their warning to ambitious candidates is blunt: challenging for the nomination could amount to a “suicide mission” because any nominee would have to defend President Donald Trump’s record, satisfy an unpredictable MAGA loyalty test and somehow persuade voters who just rejected the party in the 2026 midterms.

The retreat is not yet a formal party strategy. Republicans still expect to field a nominee and spend heavily. But the assessments reported by AlterNet, drawing on interviews published by The Hill, show a party confronting the political cost of binding its identity to one leader while remaining unable to break with him.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

A record candidates cannot defend or disown

One GOP source identified the trap facing prospective candidates: criticizing an incumbent president who retains substantial influence over Republican voters could be fatal in a primary, while defending his policies could be fatal in a general election.

“How can a candidate run in 2028 when they have to criticize the policies of a sitting president with a large amount of sway with the Republican base?” the source told The Hill. “It’s a suicide mission.”

The same source said a credible Republican campaign would require a major change in national conditions, including an end to the war in Iran, lower gas and grocery costs, and a White House perceived as attentive to voters’ needs. Without that reversal, the source argued, the party’s better opportunity may come in 2032, when Trump is “no longer a factor.”

That diagnosis assigns responsibility more honestly than the party’s fallback hope that Democrats will rescue Republicans by governing badly. The problems operatives listed are attached to the administration currently exercising power: war, household costs and public dissatisfaction with the White House. Waiting for the opposition to stumble is not a governing agenda. It is an admission that Republican strategists do not expect their own leadership to repair the damage quickly enough.

Vance confronts the cost of succession

Vice President J.D. Vance, the most obvious heir to the administration, is reportedly reconsidering a 2028 campaign. A former Trump aide told The Hill that “it may not be his time,” citing the scale of the party’s midterm defeat. AlterNet also reports that Vance received a new assignment amid continuing fallout from the Iran war, though the account does not specify the role.

Veteran Republican strategist Susan Del Percio said Vance’s political future is uncertain and suggested that the absence of Trump’s endorsement could furnish him with a face-saving reason not to run. Trump has not endorsed Vance or another prospective candidate.

The predicament extends beyond one vice president. Del Percio said any Republican nominee would be required to appear “100 percent MAGA” and pass a loyalty test whose terms can change with Trump’s preferences. That is the institutional consequence of a party organized around personal obedience rather than a stable platform: no successor can confidently inherit the coalition because its defining authority remains with the person at the top.

“Trump will be the downfall of any 2028 nominee,” Del Percio said, adding that his political standing could deteriorate further. Her forecast remains an assessment, not an established outcome. But the hesitation among would-be candidates shows that Republican professionals already regard Trump’s continued control as a liability they lack the power—or willingness—to confront.

The plan is to wait for Democrats to fail

Republican strategists have not accepted conceding the election. Instead, they reportedly hope that Democrats, after taking control of Congress, will produce enough mistakes and internal conflict to improve the GOP’s position. Some operatives also see room for recovery despite historically Republican states flipping in the midterms.

Still, the private outlook is bleak. One consultant who worked on midterm races said party officials remain in “the fog of defeat” and do not expect conditions to improve substantially by 2028. Republicans will compete and “spend a ton of money,” the consultant said, but few believe reclaiming the White House or reversing the loss of major institutions is realistically within reach.

Money, then, is not the missing ingredient. The party expects to have plenty of it. What it lacks is a politically viable way to separate itself from the administration’s record without provoking the president and the base he still commands.

The operatives urging candidates to wait until 2032 are not proposing a correction. They are proposing endurance: preserve personal careers, hope Democrats create an opening and postpone the reckoning until Trump’s grip weakens. That may be rational advice for Republican aspirants. It is also a damning description of a governing party whose prospective leaders see no safe way to defend their president, challenge him or succeed him.

item.title: Trump biographer assumes everything being said publicly is probably the opposite
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Michael Wolff’s answer to the federal government’s explanation of a nationwide aviation breakdown was blunt: assume the opposite. Speaking Saturday with Joanna Coles on a Daily Beast podcast, the Trump biographer argued that officials’ public assurances about a Microsoft outage and an FAA failure were so untrustworthy that their denial of a connection made him suspect one. That is a judgment about institutional credibility, not evidence that the failures were connected. AlterNet’s report establi
item.content:encoded:
Michael Wolff’s answer to the federal government’s explanation of a nationwide aviation breakdown was blunt: assume the opposite. Speaking Saturday with Joanna Coles on a Daily Beast podcast, the Trump biographer argued that officials’ public assurances about a Microsoft outage and an FAA failure were so untrustworthy that their denial of a connection made him suspect one.

That is a judgment about institutional credibility, not evidence that the failures were connected. AlterNet’s report establishes no such link. What it does reveal is a government asking the public to trust its crisis management while offering shifting spending demands, blaming inadequate technology and confronting reported concerns about the contractor entrusted with modernizing critical air-traffic systems.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Reassurance without an accounting

According to AlterNet, Markwayne Mullin opened a Friday news conference by saying the Microsoft and FAA failures were unrelated, assuring the public that the incident was not another September 11 and urging people not to panic. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy attributed the disruption to poor technology and used the breakdown to press for additional FAA funding.

Wolff treated the denial itself as incriminating. “It’s a fair chance the opposite is the truth,” he said, arguing that the officials had exhausted their credibility. After a clip in which the government claimed, “We’re built to handle crisis,” Wolff replied: “We’re built to create crises.”

The line is effective because it captures the governing contradiction on display: officials responsible for the system presented themselves as reassuring bystanders to its failure. But Wolff’s suspicion does not establish causation. His theory—that officials either did not understand what happened or understood and would not admit it—remained a theory. The stronger indictment lies in what the government’s own response reportedly showed: no clear public accounting of why the aviation system failed, paired with an immediate demand for more money.

A crisis becomes a funding pitch

AlterNet reports that the administration’s proposed additional FAA funding moved through a series of figures. An initial request for $15 billion became $19 billion. President Donald Trump then sought another $30 billion, and Duffy said he wanted the total increased to $50 billion, on top of $12.5 billion already provided.

A failing system may genuinely require major investment. Air-traffic infrastructure is not repaired through austerity or slogans. But rapidly changing price tags do not explain what failed, who was responsible or how new spending would prevent a recurrence. Duffy’s appeal converted operational chaos into leverage before the public received a coherent diagnosis.

That is not proof that the request was illegitimate. It is evidence of an administration asking Congress and the public to accept urgency in place of specificity. The people controlling the agency, its contracts and its budget proposal hold the power to produce that specificity. Travelers stranded by a ground stop do not.

Modernization entrusted to a troubled contractor

The funding argument also runs through Peraton, the contractor selected to take over FAA modernization. AlterNet cites an August Politico report in which three FAA officials expressed serious concerns about the company’s performance.

One person familiar with internal discussions said Peraton had “basically not done any work since they got in,” faulting it for failing to manage subcontractors and allowing an Alaska project to slip behind schedule. An industry official offered a more vivid account: at one radar work site, a Peraton manager allegedly brought doughnuts and sat in a corner instead of ensuring that other contractors performed their duties.

The criticism was not one-directional. The officials also reportedly accused the FAA itself of obstructing Peraton’s work. That points to an institutional failure broader than one inattentive manager: a federal agency and its chosen contractor blaming each other while the infrastructure they are supposed to modernize remains vulnerable.

The reported contractor problems do not prove that Peraton caused the Microsoft outage, the FAA failure or the ground stop. AlterNet does not establish that connection. They do, however, complicate Duffy’s attempt to package the episode simply as a technology problem requiring a larger appropriation. Technology does not neglect schedules, mismanage contractors or stonewall modernization. People and institutions do.

Distrust is the result, not the evidence

Coles called the officials a “ship of fools.” Wolff suggested that disrupted staffing, underfunding and unfilled jobs may have left them unable to understand the crisis—or that they knew more than they disclosed. The supplied reporting does not resolve that choice.

Nor does it justify Wolff’s shortcut that official statements should be inverted automatically. Governments can destroy their credibility through evasions, contradictions and visible incompetence, but disbelief is not an investigative method. If officials say two failures were unrelated, the responsible challenge is to demand the technical basis for that claim, not declare the reverse true by reflex.

Still, Wolff’s cynicism did not arise in a vacuum. Officials reportedly met a nationwide disruption with reassurance, blame and an expanding funding request, while earlier warnings described paralysis between the FAA and a major contractor. The administration may eventually provide a convincing explanation. In the account AlterNet published, it had instead offered the public an assurance of competence from the same institutions whose conduct made that assurance difficult to credit.

item.title: Trump legal foe sees common fight in Mississippi ballots and DC arch
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Norm Eisen argues that Scott Colom’s reported Mississippi Senate victory and the legal fight against President Donald Trump’s proposed 25-story arch reflect the same political contest: whether officials can impose consequential decisions until courts, voters or organized opponents force them to stop. In an essay for The Contrarian reported by AlterNet, Eisen cast both developments as administration losses and evidence that resistance can still constrain executive power. That conclusion is politi
item.content:encoded:
Norm Eisen argues that Scott Colom’s reported Mississippi Senate victory and the legal fight against President Donald Trump’s proposed 25-story arch reflect the same political contest: whether officials can impose consequential decisions until courts, voters or organized opponents force them to stop. In an essay for The Contrarian reported by AlterNet, Eisen cast both developments as administration losses and evidence that resistance can still constrain executive power.

That conclusion is political advocacy, not a neutral accounting. But the cases he describes share a concrete institutional pattern. In Mississippi, restrictive voting rules and a purge based on allegedly outdated data complicated access to the ballot and delayed the count. In Washington, Trump’s administration moved ahead with changes to federal land while challengers argued that the president was claiming authority belonging to Congress.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Mississippi made voting harder, then treated the delay as procedure

Colom won despite Mississippi’s unusually narrow voting options, according to Eisen, who said he worked with a voting-rights coalition opposing state officials’ efforts. Mississippi is one of three states without early in-person voting and one of 13 requiring an excuse to vote by mail. For most residents, Election Day is therefore the only chance to cast a ballot, and polling places close at 7 p.m.

Those restrictions do not distribute inconvenience evenly. Eisen wrote that long lines fall particularly heavily on Black communities. The state controls the rules, the timetable and the machinery of registration; voters bear the cost in missed work, travel, waiting time and the risk that an administrative problem will prevent an ordinary ballot from being counted.

That imbalance became especially consequential after Mississippi partnered with Experian and used what Eisen described as outdated information to remove more than 230,000 voters from the rolls this year. The purge produced thousands of provisional ballots—called “affidavit” ballots in Mississippi—that required additional review before counting. Eisen said that process explains why the result took so long.

The delay, then, was not simply electoral fog. Under Eisen’s account, it was a foreseeable result of decisions made by state officials: restrict alternatives to Election Day, remove an enormous number of registrations using unreliable information, and then subject affected voters to slower verification. Colom’s victory did not erase those burdens. It showed that voters could overcome them in this race, not that the system was defensible.

Eisen said Mississippi now has an opportunity to simplify its voting rules. More precisely, state officials have an opportunity to stop manufacturing obstacles and calling the resulting complications administrative necessity.

The arch dispute is a fight over who gets to decide

Eisen’s group is also seeking to block Trump’s proposed 25-story arch, a project AlterNet described as including a sniper’s nest and a cafe. Work on the proposal was paused during the week covered by the report, and Eisen said his group had moved to join the litigation on behalf of nine Kennedy family members.

Their objections concern both physical consequences and constitutional authority. The challengers argue that the structure would obstruct historically important sight lines, cast shadows over American soldiers’ graves and damage the setting of Kennedy family gravesites. Eisen said the group submitted declarations from family members detailing that impact.

The legal argument reaches beyond the architecture: the challengers contend that Congress, not Trump, has the power to decide whether the arch can be built. That separation-of-powers claim identifies the central issue more clearly than debate over the monument’s appearance. A president’s enthusiasm for a project does not itself create legal authority to place it on federal land.

The Kennedy family’s involvement supplies emotional and historical weight, but the institutional question should not depend on a famous name. If Congress holds the relevant power, the administration cannot cure an unauthorized decision by making the proposed structure grander, more symbolic or more personally important to the president.

Public land became another pressure point

A related case concerns East Potomac Park, where the administration planned to close an island containing parks, trails and a golf course to the public on November 15. The government cited a dangerous, deteriorating seawall and the absence of anyone to manage the course after the administration canceled the operator’s contract.

Eisen said the dispute returned to court on Friday and that his legal group was awaiting a judge’s decision on whether to halt the closure. The seawall concern may be legitimate; the supplied reporting does not resolve that factual question. But the administration’s own cancellation of the management contract is part of the sequence, not an external event that simply happened to it. Officials cannot make an operational decision and then describe its consequences as though no one exercised agency.

The Mississippi ballot fight, the East Potomac closure and the proposed arch are not identical cases. One concerns state election administration, another public access and infrastructure, and the third presidential authority over a monumental construction project. Eisen joins them as examples of successful resistance to government action.

The narrower lesson is stronger than the slogan. Institutional power rarely checks itself. In Mississippi, voters had to navigate rules officials chose to maintain. In Washington, litigants had to ask a court to prevent closures or construction decisions from taking effect. The reported victories belong not to a system functioning automatically, but to people forced to spend time, money and legal effort making officials answer for choices those officials had the power to avoid.
